t: A pending order no longer depends on the date it happens to carry
n: HE ASKED WHY SOME CUSTOMERS' PENDING ORDERS APPEARED AND OTHERS' DID NOT, and the answer was the worst kind: nothing to do with policy. CA5-KER's pending order is dated 28 Jul so it fell inside the window and showed; CI4-OKR's is dated 03 Aug so the 02 Aug cut-off silently dropped it. Two customers in identical positions were getting different statements for a reason neither could have seen.

A pending order is an open commitment, not an event inside a period, and it is still open on the day the statement is issued whatever date sits on the row. stmtRows now applies the from/to window to everything EXCEPT pending orders, which are always included.

The period line follows, or the document contradicts itself. A statement headed 'to 02 Aug' carrying a row dated 03 Aug is exactly the small inconsistency that costs more trust than the figure it hides, so where a pending order falls outside the window the line now reads 'to 02 Aug 2026, plus any order agreed and not yet actioned'. Where none does, it is unchanged, and CA5-KER's statement is untouched.

The run now ties to the ledger exactly, less gifts. Desk-wide order value RM12,923.26 against the run's RM12,590.00, the whole RM333.26 difference being gifts carried at nil across CJ4-BJ, CJ4-OKR and CS6-BS. There is no longer any timing difference to explain. Within the run, RM12,590.00 ordered less RM11,895.00 paid leaves RM695.00, being RM310.00 outstanding and RM385.00 agreed but not yet actioned. Three customers now hold a pending order, up from two.

t: A cancelled order was being billed on the statement
n: HE SPOTTED IT: CC5-OKR should read as two completed orders and one cancelled, and the statement was showing three orders, RM270 ordered, RM90 outstanding and 1 unit owed. The 20 Jul order was agreed at RM90 and cancelled the next day with nothing moved either way; its own ledger note says 'counts nowhere'.

txStat has returned 'Cancelled' since long before statements existed. stmtRows simply never asked, so a cancelled order fell through to the ordinary path and was billed like any other. The desk's own aggregates were always right, which is why this never showed anywhere but here. Same class of fault as the pending-order bug at v189, found the same way: by reading the whole run rather than one file.

A cancelled order now carries no money owed and no goods owed, and counts in NOTHING: not value, not quantity, not the number of orders. It stays on the page struck through and labelled with its cancellation date, because he agreed to it and remembers it, and a statement that silently drops it invites the question it exists to answer. The footer says '2 orders, 2 unit, 1 cancelled, not counted' so the count cannot disagree with the total beside it.

The whole run was then reconciled against the ledger rather than eyeballed. Desk-wide order value RM12,923.26 against the statement run's RM12,405.00, a difference of RM518.26, fully explained: RM333.26 of gifts carried at nil across CJ4-BJ, CJ4-OKR and CS6-BS, plus one CI4-OKR order dated 03 Aug which a statement issued 02 Aug correctly excludes. Within the run, RM12,405.00 ordered less RM11,895.00 paid leaves RM510.00, being RM310.00 outstanding and RM200.00 agreed but not actioned.
Goods owed across the whole run is now nil. The 1 unit previously shown was the phantom from that cancelled order.

t: A settlement walk that printed zeros, and the leak test brought in from the cold
n: CS6-PER's statement was unintelligible and was about to be sent. The settlement walk was written for the case where salt is withheld to clear unpaid balances on earlier ORDERS, and it assumes those orders exist. His 6.5 unit went against a cash advance, which is not in the sales ledger, so the walk found nothing to reconcile and printed a table of zeros: 'carried forward 0.00', then '0.00 at 0.00 a unit is 6.5 unit'. stmtRecon now flags the no-leg case and stmtDoc states it plainly instead: the order was paid in full, 6.5 unit was held back by agreement against a separate arrangement, and the balance was collected. It does not name the arrangement, which is not a statement's business, and it invites the question instead.
The row label followed. It read '6.5 unit applied to an earlier balance', contradicting the explanation three inches below it; where there are no legs it now reads 'applied by agreement'.

THE LEAK TEST NOW LIVES IN THE PROJECT, at 05_Pricing/leak_test.js. It had been a scratch file and was lost when that folder was cleared, which is the wrong place for the one check standing between the ledger and a customer's phone. Rebuilding it exposed how easily it cries wolf, and both faults are fixed and written down: it strips style and script before matching, because a stylesheet says margin:0 on every block and reporting that as a leaked margin trains you to skim past a real one; it matches only the two-decimal money form, because bare integers collide with font sizes and dates; it does not count a parent code found on its own sub-account's file, since CS6-BS-1-MK contains CS6-BS by construction; and it does not call a cost a leak when it equals a rate the customer himself paid, which is how CS6-PER's RM60 rate was first reported.

Statements regenerated against v191's repricing. CA4-DAM's order is now paid and collected, so the run reads 12,495.00 ordered against 11,895.00 paid, and the 600.00 gap is exactly 400.00 outstanding plus 200.00 agreed but not yet actioned. 25 files, all clean.

t: A one-step same-day trail folds into its opening, and the test for doing it is written down
n: Two things flagged on the v190 run are fixed here. Neither moves a figure; both are about the desk saying the same thing twice.

THE CZ4-TBC ORDER OF 30 JUL carried an amendment trail of exactly one step, dated on the order date, restating what the row already said: RM435 and 5 unit, paid and collected on the day it was agreed. The standing rule is that a settlement on the order date folds into the OPENING LINE rather than becoming a movement, so the ledger card was rendering Opened, then a movement identical to the opening, then Closed, for a transaction that only ever moved once. The trail is deleted; deliveredOn and paidOn were already stated on the row, so txDates() still dates it from a stated field rather than assuming. The canonical figures were always what recompute() read, so revenue, cash, margin and stock are untouched: RM12,538, RM11,682, RM4,567 at 36.4% and 72.65 unit, all unchanged. The only movement is in the Analysis dating attribution, where the walk now reaches the counted figure on 13 orders dated from a trail and 12 from an explicit deliveredOn, against 14 and 11 before. The walk still never goes below zero and still foots to 72.65 unit.

THE MORE USEFUL HALF IS THE TEST. A scan of the book found sixteen amendment steps dated on their own order date, across fifteen rows, and the obvious reading would have folded all of them. That would have been a serious fault. replayAmend starts from cumCash=0 and cumKg=0 and accumulates, so in a multi-step trail the first step IS the opening: strip it and every later state is understated by exactly what the opening moved, an order that closed would read Open and a completed one Partial. THE TEST IS THE WHOLE TRAIL, NOT THE STEP. Fold only where the ENTIRE trail is a single step on the order date. One row met that test; the other fourteen open on the order date and are correct as they stand, and are deliberately left alone. The rule is now written into the source above replayAmend so the next run does not have to rediscover it, and into the daily task file.

THE DAILY TASK FILE described a sixteen-tab desk with a Version control tab. That tab went at v177 when the changelog moved to 04_Docs. The desk has rendered fifteen tabs since, so the instruction was asking each run to verify a tab that does not exist. Corrected to fifteen, with the reason and an instruction to count the rendered tabs before asserting a number. Also corrected there: the duplicated frontmatter block, the missing 07_Statements folder, the stamp step still saying it adds a Version control entry when it prepends to 04_Docs/changelog.json, and a note that sales and purchases are top-level const in a classic script and must be reached from jsdom with window.eval rather than window.sales, which reads undefined and looks like a broken desk.

t: The CA4-DAM order is repriced, paid and collected on its own day

The RM10 concession crossed a line the RM110 did not, and the previous note on this row had said as much before it was conceded.

Five orders in, he has now paid exactly RM100/unit four times. That makes RM100 his standing rate rather than a one-off, which is the thing to settle before a sixth order rather than after it. He was one of the two customers P2 grandfathered for one more order at his old rate; that order has now been taken.

t: Pending orders on a statement, and a review sheet for the monthly run
n: The monthly statement run showed PENDING ORDERS AS OUTSTANDING. CA4-DAM, CA5-KER, CC5-OKR and CH5-KLC each read as owing money on an order where nothing had been paid and nothing collected. The desk has counted pending nowhere since v111; the statement builder was quietly breaking that rule, and these files go out to customers. Fixed at source in stmtRows: a pending order carries owed 0 and a pendingOrder flag.

Correcting it exposed the opposite fault. With owed at zero the row fell through to 'settled', which is worse: it tells a customer an order he is still waiting for is closed. Pending now has its own status, 'ordered / to be collected and paid', and the totals carry a plain line saying how much of the ordered figure has not yet happened. CA4-DAM now reads 485.00 ordered, 375.00 paid, 110.00 not yet collected, balance nil, and the three figures tie without him having to ask.
Pending is also excluded from goods owed. Nothing has been paid for, so nothing is being withheld.

Review sheet added at 05_Pricing/make_statements.js: _review_<issue>.html stitches all 24 statements behind an index, so the whole run can be read in one pass before anything is sent. It lifts the stylesheet from the first statement rather than carrying its own, so a restyle cannot leave the two versions of the truth out of step. The index now has a 'Not actioned' column; across the run, outstanding 400.00 plus not actioned 310.00 accounts exactly for the 710.00 gap between 12,505.00 ordered and 11,795.00 paid.

The leak test exempts the review sheet from the other-party check, since containing every account is its purpose, but still applies the 14 seller-only terms, all cost and margin figures and every internal note fragment to it. 25 files, all clean.

t: Monthly statements for every customer, filed and scheduled (02 Aug, first Sunday). The first full month is closed, so the desk now issues a statement of account per customer and keeps them. Twenty-four written to 07_Statements\\2026-08, the year-month folder sorting chronologically under an alphabetical sort and the code in each filename sorting the customers inside it. One gap closed first: refunds. The statement had no line for money returned, which is something a customer certainly knows about and whose omission ran in only one direction. CZ6-WM’s RM80 overpayment now appears on his, dated and marked paid. And a label corrected: a free unit showed as goodwill, but the same flag covers a reseller’s EARNED reward, and calling an earned reward a gift misdescribes it to the one person who knows better. Both now read no charge. The generator drives the desk rather than copying it. 05_Pricing\\make_statements.js loads the desk headlessly and calls its own stmtRows, stmtRefunds, stmtRecon and stmtDoc, so the rules for what a customer may see exist in exactly one place and the batch cannot drift from the tab. Each statement covers everything to date rather than the month alone: a complete position is more use than a slice, and it removes the brought-forward problem entirely. The month is what the folder records. Every file is proved before it is trusted. All 24 were checked against 27 other parties, 14 seller-only terms, 94 cost and margin figures and 85 internal note fragments. All clean. Scheduled for midnight on the first Sunday of each month, and the gate is worth recording: cron cannot express that, because restricting both day-of-month and day-of-week is an OR in most implementations and would have fired on all seven first days AND every Sunday. So it runs every Sunday and stops immediately unless the date is 1 to 7.

CJ4-BJ is closed with 4.75 unit, and CA4-DAM opens at RM110 (01 Aug). The 4.1912 he was owed went out, closing the 15 Jul order and every account between them, and 0.5588 unit went out on top as goodwill, taking him to the 4.75 he had asked for. The gift is on its own row and not folded into the order, because inflating the order’s quantity would have stopped it matching what was agreed, which is the very thing the reconciliation exists to prove. It is booked in-kind AT COST, RM26.26, not at his RM68 selling rate. Recording it at all matters: salt leaving the shelf with no line against it books as shrinkage, and a deliberate gift is not a loss, which is why the plug stays at 26.05 unit. Valuing it at cost matters as much: at the selling rate it would have carried RM11.74 of margin, so a giveaway would have improved gross margin, which is plainly wrong. At cost, revenue and expense are the same figure and margin is untouched at RM4,514; what the gift costs shows where it should, in salt no longer on the shelf. Stated for the record: the desk was not shown to be wrong. The 25 Jul offset of 2.0588 unit was agreed and evidenced; conceding the difference is a commercial choice about a relationship, not an accounting correction. Two faults the closure surfaced in the statement. The gift’s in-kind value was counting as a PAYMENT, so Paid read RM1,566.26 against RM1,540 ordered, which is the one arithmetic a reader would certainly catch; a gift is now excluded from paid and shows as nil, goodwill, no charge. And the reconciliation announced How the 0 unit is arrived at once nothing was owed; it now reads How your 15 Jul order was settled and shifts to the past tense, because after a dispute the proof is worth more than during one. And CA4-DAM: 1 unit at RM110, pending. The number to price against is not the headline but the fact that he always collects. Delivery is assumed at RM17.50 a lot, so a collected order retains every ringgit: RM110 from him is worth RM127.50 from someone driven to, and against the R card’s RM120 delivered, which nets RM102.50, this is already the better trade by RM7.50. His own history is four orders at a median RM100/unit, so RM110 sits 10% above his established rate, and dropping to RM100 would both return him to it and put him under what the R card nets.

The statement now shows its working, because a figure does not settle a dispute (01 Aug). It said 4.19 unit and explained it in a sentence, which asks the customer to take it on trust. He cannot check a conclusion; he can check a chain. So the statement now reconstructs the whole thing from the ledger, in four numbered steps. One: the earlier orders that were short, as a small table — 28 Jun billed RM600 against RM550 paid in cash, RM50 short; 05 Jul billed RM90 against nothing paid, RM90 short; RM140 carried forward. Two: that RM140 settled out of the 15 Jul order in salt rather than cash, at RM140 over RM68 a unit, being 2.06 unit withheld. Three: the 15 Jul order itself paid in full, RM650 on 15 Jul and RM200 on 01 Aug. Four: bought 12.5, less 2.06 applied to the balance, deliverable 10.44, less 6.25 collected, 4.19 still to collect. Every figure is derived, not quoted: the shortfalls are read off the referenced orders, and the rate is obtained by dividing the balance by the salt withheld, so it cannot disagree with the lines above it. The unit rate is now shown, reversing v184 deliberately. A conversion of money into goods cannot be proved without naming the rate it used. It appears only inside a reconciliation and only on the order carrying the offset. And the one contradiction a careful reader would find is answered before he finds it: those two orders read as settled at the top while showing short in the workings, so a closing line says plainly that their balance was cleared here in salt rather than in cash and nothing about them is owed in money. The leak test still passes: no other party, no cost, no margin, no note text.

CJ4-BJ pays the final RM200, and what he is owed is now salt (01 Aug). The order is PAID IN FULL at RM850, and the dispute is about the other side of it, so the desk states the figure and its workings rather than the figure alone. He is owed 4.1912 unit. The arithmetic, in the order it happened: he bought 12.5 unit at RM68, which is RM850; on 25 Jul 2.0588 unit was withheld by agreement to settle the RM140 he had left unpaid on the 28 Jun and 05 Jul orders, that being RM140 at his own RM68 rate, so his deliverable is 10.4412 unit rather than 12.5; he has taken 6.25 unit; and 10.4412 less 6.25 is 4.1912. Every account between them closes when that salt is handed over. The statement now leads with it. A document whose only large figure is money reads as though nothing is outstanding, which is exactly the misreading a dispute about undelivered goods turns on. So goods owed get their own block, in its own colour, with the workings written out: ordered, less what was applied to the earlier balance, less what has been collected. He can check every step against his own record without being told the answer. The line itself now reads paid in full with 4.19 unit still to collect beneath it, rather than the bare settled that a fully paid order would otherwise have shown. What moved on the desk: collected rises to RM11,582, revenue to RM12,412 as the RM200 pending slice becomes real (2.94 unit at his rate, which is the same RM200 seen from the other side), salt owed out rises to 4.19 unit and free to sell falls to 74.21. Receivables are unchanged at RM248, because his RM200 was a pending slice rather than an advance. The leak test still passes.

The statement says less, and reads better for it (01 Aug). The first cut carried a price-per-unit column and a running commentary on every line: paid this, collected that, settled together with the order of such a date. All of it was true and none of it was wanted. A customer opening this wants three things — what he took, when, and how much — and every extra column asks him to work out which ones matter. So the line is now date, quantity, amount, status, and nothing else, with the payment date as a quiet second line only where it differs from the order date. The unit price went with the rest, and that was the point worth arguing. It told him nothing he did not already know, and it made his own rate legible in a single portable document, which is the sort of thing that ends up beside another buyer’s. Totals say what he paid; the arithmetic is his to do if he wants it. The design does the work the columns were doing: a narrow measure, generous line spacing, tabular figures that align down the column, the amount carrying the weight, a status that is one quiet word, and a summary that ends on the only number he came for. It prints on white without being redesigned. The leak test still passes against every other party, twelve seller-only terms, the cost and margin figures for those orders, and every note fragment. CJ4-BJ’s statement is now three lines and a total: 19.5 unit, RM1,540 ordered, RM1,340 paid, RM200 outstanding.

A customer can now be handed his own record (01 Aug). One asked for it, and it is a permanent feature: pick a party on the Ledger tab, set an optional date range, tick what to include, and export a self-contained Statement of account. The whole design is about what it must NOT contain. This is the only artefact that leaves the desk describing a named party’s dealings, so it is built rather than copied. Every note in this ledger is written for him and several are about his own bookkeeping — recorded as 9.47 delivered in error, the RM200 booked as received was NEVER PAID, delivery audit. None of that is the buyer’s business, and no filter over free text is safe enough to be trusted with it. So the statement is assembled from the order itself: date, quantity, unit price, total, what was paid and when, what was collected and when, what remains. Nothing else can travel with it, at any setting: no cost, no margin, no shrinkage or replacement rate, no tier or floor, no other party, and not one character of the internal notes. A test proves it rather than the comment claiming it: a generated statement is checked against every other party on the roster, twelve seller-only terms in the visible text, the cost and margin FIGURES for those very orders, and the opening fragment of every note attached to them. It passes clean. What he does get is what he already knows: what he ordered, what he agreed to pay, what he handed over, what he collected, and the balance between them. An in-kind settlement is included because he agreed to it, stated as an amount and a date rather than with the reasoning that sits behind it here, and a cross-reference names only the DATE of another of his own orders. His real name is off by default and needs the vault open; it is the one name that belongs on the document, since it is going to him, and no other party appears at any setting. The first one is generated for CJ4-BJ: three orders, RM1,540 ordered, RM1,200 paid in cash, RM140 settled in kind, RM200 outstanding.

One pending order, and it is worth a second look (01 Aug). CH5-KLC has agreed 0.5 unit at RM80 for 31 Jul. Nothing is paid and nothing delivered, so it is PENDING and counts nowhere: revenue holds at RM12,212, collected at RM11,382 and the shelf at 78.4 unit. Pending rises to 6.44 unit across four orders worth RM585. The price is not a concession, and it is still worth questioning. RM160/unit is the M card exactly for a half unit, so it sits on the ladder rather than under it. But his FIRST order paid RM210/unit — the best rate this desk has ever achieved, and the very figure the lot outlook uses as its ceiling at this size. Agreeing RM160 with the one buyer who proved RM210 gives away RM25 on a half unit, at the most profitable size the desk sells. He may simply not pay RM210 twice, and that is worth finding out deliberately rather than discovering it after RM160 has become his standing rate. The desk does not flag this as a breach, because it is not one: it clears every floor and matches a card. It is a pricing judgement, which is why it is written into the order rather than into Boundaries.

The server now stops ten seconds after the desk closes, without ever stopping while it is open (31 Jul). He asked for ten seconds. The naive version of that is a ten-second idle limit, and it would have been a trap: browsers throttle timers in a background tab to roughly once a minute, so a desk sitting behind another window would miss every beat and be read as closed. He would have lost the server while still using it, which is a worse fault than the one being fixed. So the beat now reports what the page is doing and the server keeps two limits. Visible, beating every three seconds, ten seconds of silence really does mean gone. Hidden, a long limit applies, because a throttled beat is not evidence of anything. Switching tabs cannot kill it, and coming back beats immediately rather than waiting for the next tick. A real close does not wait for any limit at all: pagehide fires a sendBeacon to /bye and the server stops on its next one-second tick, measured at 0.6s. The limits are only the fallback for a browser that never fires the event. One guard worth its line: pagehide also fires when a page enters the back/forward cache, which is a navigation and not a close, so event.persisted now tells them apart and a bfcache suspend no longer shuts the server on him. Verified on all four paths: a visible desk that stops beating dies in 11.6s; a hidden one survives 16s of total silence and only stops at its own long limit; an explicit goodbye stops it in 0.6s; and silence during the startup grace does not kill it before the browser has even loaded.

What each lot can still earn, and the cash balance goes (31 Jul). A per-lot outlook now sits on Sourcing, carrying a ceiling and an expectation for the salt still on the shelf, exactly as he asked. The ceiling is evidence, and it respects the ladder. A first cut priced every remaining unit at the best rate ever paid, RM210/unit, which reached RM18,589 of revenue. That rate was achieved on a HALF UNIT, and pricing eighty of them at a half-unit rate sets a target nobody will pay, which is worse than no target: an unreachable ceiling is only a way of feeling behind. So the shelf is split the way his orders have actually split, and each slice is priced at the best HIS OWN BOOK has achieved at that size. It blends to RM111.11/unit and RM9,836 of revenue against an expected RM6,815, and it means something he can chase: if every order from here matched his own best for its size. The expectation is what the book has been doing, RM86.53/unit across the observed mix, less the 11% leakage, and it carries the order count and the spread behind it so the estimate shows its own confidence. That is the part that sharpens: every priced sale moves the average and narrows the spread, so accuracy is earned from trade rather than asserted by a model. The gap splits three ways, not two. RM845 is salt that never reaches a customer, worth that at today's prices. RM1,936 is the salt that does, sold under a rate already proven. And RM213 comes only from doing both, being the better price on the units the leak would have eaten. My own check caught that a two-part split failed to sum to the whole by exactly that third term, so it is named rather than buried: a decomposition that does not add up is worth less than none. The same check caught a second fault. Reconstructing what was left by subtracting deliveries and a share of the plug gave 88.52 unit against a counted 78.4. On this desk the count always wins, so the counted stock is now ALLOCATED across lots, newest first, and the lot totals tie to it by construction. And the cash balance is gone entirely, at his instruction. He wants flow, not balance, and he is right that the balance was never the desk's to know: it needed an opening figure nobody remembered, a count to work backwards from, and a reconciliation of undocumented drawings. Each was a place for a wrong number to enter and be inherited downstream, which is how a RM200 overstatement survived four versions. The desk now states only what trading moved: RM11,382 in, RM12,650 out, RM1,348 net. Every balance readout is replaced by the flow, and the counted-balance panel is removed rather than left unreachable.

His pending order comes back, and the input fault is fully confirmed (31 Jul). He asked where his pending CI4-OKR order had gone, and the answer was that I had destroyed it. The truth is simpler than either reading I had tried: the Monday order was never 5 unit. It was written down as 5 unit / RM440 and was always 2 unit / RM185; his 31 Jul amendment was a clerical correction of the terms, nothing more. Nothing was paid, nothing was collected, and the order stays PENDING for 03 Aug. This confirms the input bug exactly. The Modification fields were labelled Cash moved and Salt moved, so when he typed the corrected quantity and total the desk read them as money and salt changing hands. His entry was right; the form mislabelled it, and I then compounded it twice: first booking a part-fulfilment of a 5 unit order, then a completed 2 unit sale. Both errors have the same root, fixed at v177, where a Modification now asks for the NEW total and NEW quantity and carries no cash or kg at all. What moves back: revenue falls to RM12,212 and collected to RM11,382, because RM185 that was never received had been counted; the 2 unit return to the shelf, taking stock to 78.4 unit and free to sell to 77.15; and pending rises to 5.94 unit across three orders worth RM505. The lesson is about the desk, not the trade. A form that labels one field two different ways depending on a dropdown will be misread, and the ledger will faithfully record the misreading. The fix was to make the field say what it means.

A restatement that moved money left its card looking unfinished (31 Jul). He asked why two pending-looking ledger rows were drawn differently, and one of the three reasons was a bug of mine from v177. Two are by design. An order WITH an amendment trail renders as a card, headed by the line it Opened on and closed by a Closed line; an order without one is a single row labelled Open, so the two words are a header and a whole row rather than two states. And a fully pending order carries no date at all, by the v111 rule, because a date on something that has not happened is a claim; the other order is no longer fully pending, so it shows one. The third was mine. v177 correctly stopped a Modification carrying cash and kg, since a restatement moves nothing. But the CI4-OKR trail had ONE step doing both jobs: restating the order to 2 unit for RM185 and taking the money. With no cash or kg on it the replay read the whole order as having moved nothing, so both figures greyed as carried-over and the card never produced a closing line: a completed order sat there looking pending. The fix is to record what actually happened, as two steps. A Modification that changes the terms and moves nothing, then a Fulfilment the same day for RM185 in and 2 unit out. A change of terms and a movement of goods are two events even when they share a date, and the ledger replays them in order. The card now reads Opened, pending, then Closed on 31 Jul, Completed, with a green spine. No figure moves: revenue stays RM12,397 and the order was always counted at RM185.

An amendment stops pretending to be a delivery, and the changelog leaves the desk (31 Jul). He caught a real bug. The CI4-OKR entry was an AMENDMENT, not a fulfilment, and the form could not tell the difference. Both kinds shared two number boxes labelled Cash moved and Salt moved, and whatever was typed was ADDED to what had already moved. So this order is now 2 unit at RM185 was read as 2 unit were handed over against a still-5-unit order, the preview said salt had moved when none had, and the desk then reported it as Open and Deferred because RM185 is fractionally more than 2 units' worth at the old rate. Three fixes. The labels follow the kind: a Modification asks for the NEW total and the NEW quantity, a Cancellation for what was returned, a Fulfilment for what moved. The state is read against the restated terms with movement left alone, rather than adding the two together. And the payload names its numbers, carrying newTotal and newQty with no cash or kg at all for a Modification, so nothing downstream can mistake a restatement for a movement again; the old shape used the same two keys for both and left the reader to infer it from the kind, which is exactly how this went wrong. A warning also fires if the new terms are smaller than what has already moved. The order is corrected: CI4-OKR is 2 unit for RM185, complete, and the 3 unit balance never existed. Revenue is unchanged at RM12,397, because the desk had only ever counted the RM185. And the changelog is out of the desk. 176 entries, 191 KB, 27% of the file, none of it ever read on screen. It is extracted VERBATIM to 04_Docs\\changelog.json and the Version control tab is gone; the desk falls from 710 KB to 506 KB. Nothing was rewritten, summarised or dropped, which was the instruction and is the only honest way to compress a record: the file shrank because the text MOVED, not because any of it was judged expendable. All 176 entries were checked present in the JSON before the array was replaced.

Three commits, two rows that had outstayed their welcome, and the delay explained (31 Jul). The queue, and the new route working in the wild. A party arrived through + Add ID for the first time: CA5-SEN came in already carrying his final code, so there was no placeholder and nothing to re-key, which is the whole point of v174. He bought 2.5 unit at RM270, paid and collected the same day, and that price is worth noting: RM108/unit is exactly the R card for the size, the first order on the book to take a card price without negotiation. CI4-OKR part-fulfilled early, taking 2 unit and paying RM185 on the 31st against an order agreed for Monday, so it stops being pending and now counts; 3 unit and RM255 remain open. Revenue RM12,397, collected RM11,567, margin RM4,562, shelf 76.4 unit. The settled refund is off the Order book. It was showing greyed with a paid tag, which answered the wrong question: the Order book is what is still open, and a line that is closed is history. The record stays in the data; the row goes. And the CS6-PER margin floor breach is cleared, on his instruction and on a rule rather than an exception: a thin or at-cost sale that is closed, with nothing owed and nothing left to deliver, cannot be acted on. The salt has gone and the money is in. Boundaries is a list of things to resolve, so a row that can never be resolved only teaches you to skim the list. An open thin sale still breaches, because that one can be acted on, and every one of them is still counted in full on the Pricing tab’s band analysis, which is where a lesson about price belongs. Boundaries falls to one breach. The delay opening the desk had a cause, and it was not the arithmetic. Every figure on the desk recomputes in 43ms. What cost the wait was a blocking script tag in the head fetching Chart.js from a CDN, so every open waited on the internet before the page could run, and on a poor connection or none that wait was the whole of it. A vendored copy already sits in assets/ and loads on demand, only when a tab that draws something is opened, so the tag is simply gone. A local tool should not need the internet to show a figure it already has. The watchdog now waits 15 minutes rather than 90 seconds: a background tab whose timers the browser throttles, or a machine that sleeps briefly, could miss enough beats to be killed while still in use. And the launcher runs deskctl itself, publishing and status both, so that instruction stops being repeated at him in every message. It belongs in the one moment the desk is guaranteed to be on a machine that can see both copies.

One thing to double-click, and it puts itself away (31 Jul). The launcher did one job; it now does three and then gets out of the way. It runs deskctl status first, so the version and any drift are on screen before the desk opens rather than discovered afterwards, then opens the browser, then serves the folder minimised, so nothing sits on the taskbar but a quiet box. And it stops by itself. This is the part that needed building rather than configuring: closing a browser tab tells a local server nothing — there is no event that reaches a socket — so the old server outlived the desk and sat there for the rest of the day. The desk now sends a heartbeat every 25 seconds while it is open, and the server shuts down about 90 seconds after the beats stop. On a real close the page also fires a sendBeacon, which survives the page going away where an ordinary fetch would be cancelled mid-flight, and brings the shutdown forward to a few seconds. The beacon is only a courtesy: the watchdog would notice on its own regardless, so a browser that refuses to fire the event costs a minute rather than leaving a stuck process. Two deliberate conservatisms. A two-minute grace at startup, so the watchdog cannot kill a server before the browser has even loaded the page, and a laptop waking from sleep with the desk open does not find it dead. And a merely hidden tab sends no farewell: hidden is not closed, so the beat simply continues, which is the safe reading. Closing the window by hand still works and still loses nothing. Verified by running it: the server stays up while beating, and stops nine seconds after the beats end on a shortened test limit.

A party is now born by naming it, and the four-step dance is over (31 Jul). He described the old road exactly: add new customer, then update, then save the name to the new id, then update again. Four steps, two of them mine. The cause was ordering, not effort. A proper code is derived from a name AND a place, and the Transaction tab deliberately never asks for a name, so the best it could mint was a placeholder that had to be re-keyed later. Naming first inverts that. + Add ID now sits in Names & IDs, the only panel that holds names: give the name, the location and what the party is, and the desk mints the code the ledger will carry for good. He is pushed into the live roster immediately, so his first transaction can be booked against him in the same minute, and an ADDID entry rides the queue so I bake him into the source on the next run. There is no placeholder, so there is no re-key, so the two update runs disappear. The role is part of it, as asked: customer, associate who resells (R2), referrer who introduces (R3), an associate’s end buyer, or supplier. Pick the end-buyer role and the panel asks which associate he sits under, then derives his code from the associate’s own, numbered in sequence. The location rule still bites and is stated where it bites: a name alone does not earn a code, because the place is what proves you dealt with him yourself rather than merely heard the name. The name never touches the queue. Only the code and the shape travel; the name goes straight into the encrypted vault, which is why the vault must be unlocked before an ID can be created and the panel says so rather than failing quietly. And “+ Add new” is gone from the Transaction tab, replaced by a line pointing at Add ID. Removing it is the point: an option that could only ever create work to undo is worse than no option. The derivation is the same rule the vault uses, called rather than copied, so a code minted here and a code derived from a name later are guaranteed to be the same string.

The SF6-KLC RM750 is written off, and the ladder learns to price itself (31 Jul). The write-off. He has gone unresponsive, so at 23 days and already fully provisioned the desk stops carrying the RM750 as money it expects. The provision stays charged against margin, because writing off is a change of expectation rather than a reversal of a cost; what changes is that the figure leaves the forward cash view, leaves Today and leaves Boundaries, since none of those should show a number nobody is chasing. Boundaries falls to two breaches and Today’s Now list to RM50 at stake. Any recovery is now pure upside against a book that has already taken the loss, and it must be booked as a fresh receipt rather than by un-writing this entry. CE4-CER is confirmed a typo for CE4-CHE, so the caveat comes off that sale and no phantom party was ever minted. And the ladder. He asked for pricing built from purchase cost, demand, shrinkage, delivery, buffer and margin rather than typed in once, so the Pricing tab now carries a Dynamic ladder that builds every price: effective cost times the size, plus delivery on every tier except SS which collects, plus a buffer, divided by one minus the tier margin, rounded to a multiple of ten, pulled down wherever the rate would rise with size. The margins are derived, not invented: each is what that tier’s own 1 unit price implies against today’s fully loaded cost, so the model is calibrated to his cards rather than imposed on them, and every anchor reproduces exactly. Delivery is finally recordable. deliveryLog takes actual runs and the model switches from the RM17.50 midpoint assumption to the observed mean the moment one is entered; until then it says plainly that it is an assumption. Two findings the model surfaced rather than smoothed. First, SS comes out at a flat rate per unit: it carries no per-lot delivery, so nothing in the cost gives its ladder any reason to taper, which makes the taper on the printed SS card a commercial decision rather than an arithmetic one. Second, the solver reports prices under the desk’s own floor instead of lifting them to clear it, because SS is deliberately under that floor and silencing the breach to make a ladder look tidy is the one move this desk does not make. It reprices nothing. Twenty-six of thirty-nine modelled prices differ from the printed cards, the largest by RM220 at P 6.25; the cards remain the quote board and the sheets already sent stay valid, because a board silently drifting from a sheet in a customer’s hand is the fault fixed at v165. Demand is switched off by default so the drift column shows only where arithmetic disagrees with the hand-solved taper.

A tier saves as a plain sheet, no password (31 Jul). The encrypted download at v164 is issued to one reseller, expires, and needs a code sent down a second channel. That is the right shape for a personal list and the wrong shape for the thing handed out most: a tier’s price list, the same sheet for everyone on it. So the quote board gains its plain twin. Five buttons, one per tier, each saving that ladder as a self-contained file with no password, no expiry and no script in the output. It carries the prices openly because that is the job: a customer cannot be asked for a passphrase at the counter. It follows the printed cards exactly, including the part that looks like decoration. cards.py is explicit that no card names its tier, and that the markers telling them apart are meant to be known only to him: the filename, the accent rule under the masthead, and a row of faint dots by the date, one for SS through five for P. Printing a large R on the sheet would undo that in a stroke, so the letter is in the filename and nowhere on the page. A recipient holding one sheet still learns nothing about what anyone else pays. Verified across all five: prices match the printed cards to the ringgit, the dot count is right, no page names its tier and none carries a script. The watermark is optional here, unlike the encrypted download where it is the only protection left, because a tier sheet is issued to a class and not to a person; tick the box and pick a name and it is tiled anyway. What it gives up is stated plainly on the tab: a sheet with no password cannot be withdrawn, so it should be treated as printed and will keep showing these prices until a newer one is sent. The encrypted route is unchanged and remains the one to use when a list is for a named reseller and should stop working.

CZ4-TBC has his name, and a Monday order joins the book as an intention (31 Jul). The vault first. The real name was typed against CZ4-TBC in Names and IDs and the vault saved itself: the encrypted blob is confirmed present with 27 codes mapped, and this file still carries no name anywhere, which is the whole design. The last open re-key is closed. And one queued order: CI4-OKR, 5 unit at RM440, agreed for Monday 03 Aug. Nothing paid and nothing delivered, so it is PENDING and counts nowhere: not revenue, not stock, not a receivable. Every headline figure is unchanged, which is the pending rule doing its job on a forward-dated order. Two things about it are worth the note. The price: RM88/unit clears the RM420 walk-away but sits RM20 under the R card’s RM460, a negotiated rate to a second-time buyer; his first order paid RM92.50/unit, so he has moved down the curve RM4.50 while more than doubling his size, which is roughly how a ladder is supposed to be used. The shelf: fulfilling it on Monday takes free-to-sell from 79.65 to 74.65 unit, comfortably clear of the 15 unit trigger, so no buy is forced by it.

Two bookings, a RM200 cash fault found and fixed, the buttons learn their place, and five tabs get their picture (31 Jul). The bookings first. The CZ6-WM refund is paid: RM80 out on 31 Jul, the liability clears, and the entry stays marked paid rather than vanishing, because a refund that disappeared would also delete the only record of the overpayment. The walk now treats a paid refund as trade cash leaving on its paidOn date, a kind of movement it previously had no word for. And CE4-CHE bought again: 2.5 unit at RM230, paid and delivered the same day, an exact repeat of his first order down to the ringgit. One flag on that: the instruction named the buyer CE4-CER, a code that does not exist; CE4-CHE’s only prior order is this precise size and price, so the desk booked it there as a stated assumption rather than minting a phantom party. Say the word if it was genuinely someone new. The fault the booking surfaced. Cash on hand had been overstated by exactly RM200 since v166. The E21 order carries paidOn 30 Jul, which dated its entire RM620 after the 28 Jul count, but the first RM200 tranche arrived on 14 Jul and was already inside the counted figure, so the walk re-added it. A single paidOn cannot describe money that arrived either side of a count, so the row now carries an explicit paidSplit and the walk honours it: RM200 inside the count, RM420 on top. Cash held reads RM6,120, which the arithmetic now reproduces to the ringgit. The buttons. Gold was being spent on navigation: the Today list dressed every row in the same loud button, and most of them merely changed tab to a readout, which is furniture posing as a decision. The doctrine is now explicit in the stylesheet: gold books or produces something — publish, mint, download, redeem, commit — and navigation is a quiet link that names its destination, Order book →, Overview →, so the row tells you where it leads before you commit a tap to it. And the pictures. Five tabs that were tables to the floor now open the eye first: the Order book draws every debt twice, gross and net of the provisioning ladder, so the gap between the pair is what waiting has already cost; Financials draws the year by month, revenue against gross margin; Network splits each partner into bought, sold-for-you and brought-you, which is the difference between a customer with a title and someone doing the vacant seat’s work; the Ledger draws the book day by day, ringgit written against units moved; and Sourcing draws every received lot at the rate it landed, with the defaulted lot hollow, paid and never arrived. Every chart states only what a table on its own tab already says, so a chart failing to load never hides a figure.

The CS6-PER ban is lifted formally (decided 30 Jul, pushed 31 Jul). His decision, taken after the desk flagged last night’s amendment unit as a breach and put the choice plainly: lift it and say so, or keep it and close the route. He lifted it. What that changes: the desk will accept a new order from CS6-PER again, the Transaction tab stops refusing him, and the Banned from sale row leaves Boundaries, because a lifted ban is history rather than a live standing. What it does not change: the record. The ban entry stays in PEOPLE with its dates, 26 to 30 Jul, and the note that one unit went out via amendment while it stood; deleting it would erase four days in which the desk refused a buyer and the refusal was routed around. The v167 breach flag also stands in the changelog as written, because it was true when written and it is the reason this decision got taken at all. The associate bench is a separate standing and this lift does not restore it: he may buy, and that is all. The margin floor breach on his 08 Jul package also stays, since a closed sale at cost does not reprice on anyone’s standing. Mechanically the lift is one field: the entry gains lifted 30 Jul, and isBanned, banOf and the breach generator all honour it, so nothing was deleted to make the desk agree with the decision. Boundaries reads three breaches: the CN6-WM RM50 that crossed its 10-day term today, the package margin floor, and the SF6-KLC recoverable now at 22 days.

Order CZ4-TBC completes on the day it was agreed (30 Jul). The 5 unit at RM435 that landed as PENDING earlier today was paid in full and collected the same day, so the order goes straight through: RM435 in, 5 unit out, and it now counts everywhere rather than showing in the Order book only. A single Fulfilment step is appended to the trail with cash RM435 and quantity 5 unit, and both paidOn and deliveredOn are dated 30 Jul, exactly as the CS6-BS-1-MK sale earlier today. Revenue rises to RM11,712, collected to RM10,882, margin to RM4,210 at 35.9%, and the shelf rolls to 83.4 unit with shrinkage unchanged at 26.05, because a delivery is not a loss. The price is unchanged from where it landed: RM435 is exactly the board’s own quote at this size, so no concession sits behind it. Drawn from the RM47 lot it earns RM40/unit on lot cost and RM24.06/unit against the RM62.94 replacement, so it is comfortably above both bases, unlike the RM80 single-unit sale earlier today or the RM110 associate advance on 29 Jul. No other row is touched: cost basis, receivables, cash count and supplier recoverable all stand where v167 left them.

A sale to the Melaka downstream, and the ban was breached, not lifted (30 Jul, 21:03). Two queued entries. The easy one: CS6-BS-1-MK took 2.2 unit for RM210, paid and collected the same day. RM95.45/unit sits exactly where an odd size should against the R card, between RM220 for 2 and RM270 for 2.5, and it earns RM48.45/unit on the RM47 lot it came off. Revenue rises to RM11,277, collected to RM10,447, margin to RM4,010 at 35.6%, and the shelf rolls to 88.4 unit with shrinkage unchanged at 26.05, because a delivery is not a loss. The hard one is E21. The order the RM290 closed this afternoon was restated tonight to 7.25 unit / RM620: one further unit went out to CS6-PER at RM130, paid in full on the spot. He is banned from sale, and this is a sale. The Transaction tab refuses a new order to him, and this went through as an amendment to his existing one, which is a route around the refusal rather than an exception to it. The desk’s rules on itself are clear: what happened gets booked, and what it means gets said. So the unit is in the ledger, the RM130 is in cash, and the Boundaries row now reads that the ban was breached on 30 Jul, with the next request being a refusal, rather than pretending the amendment door does not exist. On the money alone this was a clean trade: RM130 clears the walk-away at RM85, clears the R card at RM120, and nothing is owed. That is precisely why it is worth being honest about, because a breach that pays well is how a standing stops meaning anything. If the ban is over, lift it and say so; if it stands, the amendment route needs closing. That is a decision, not a figure, so the desk states it and waits.

The RM290 landed, and the new buyer has a name (30 Jul, 16:33). CS6-PER has paid. The RM290 outstanding on his repriced 6.25 unit order came in on the 30th, 16 days after delivery against a 10-day term, and it was the oldest live debt on the desk. Revenue does not move, because the sale was booked when it happened; what moves is cash collected, to RM10,107, and receivables, down to RM248 net. It was 75% provisioned, so collecting it releases RM217.50 of provision that had already been charged against margin, and debtor provisions fall from RM280 to RM63. Boundaries drops from five breaches to three, and from three watches to two. His credit cap breach and his credit age breach both clear on the payment, and so does the aged-receivable watch, because all three were statements about money that is now in. The ban does not clear, and that is the point. A ban that lifted when the debt was settled would be a debt-collection device rather than a standing, and this one is not time-limited. The rule is generated unconditionally from the banned list rather than from the balance, so paying could never have switched it off; what changed is only the wording, which used to say "keep pursuing the balance" and would have been chasing nothing. It now reads that the balance is settled and the ban stands anyway. The margin floor breach on the 08 Jul package also stands, because that is a closed sale at RM60/unit on RM60/unit cost and no later payment reprices it. And the placeholder is gone. The 5 unit pending order booked yesterday on NEW-1 is re-keyed to CZ4-TBC and the placeholder is purged outright, per the standing one-identifier rule. The order stays pending, since nothing has been paid and nothing delivered, so it still counts nowhere. Two changelog mentions of NEW-1 survive on purpose, exactly as v148 and v157 decided: they describe the format the generator produces rather than naming a party, and purging them would leave the record of the mechanism factually wrong. The vault still needs one thing from you: it opens only on your passphrase, so the real name has to be typed once against CZ4-TBC in Names and IDs. Now falls from five items to four, and the money at stake on it from RM1,040 to RM750, which is the SF6-KLC recoverable and very little else.

Four transactions committed, the five tiers become the policy, and Customers leads with what the book means (30 Jul). The queue first. Four entries, and the largest reverses a story this changelog told two versions ago. The 5 unit order that unwound has completed: CE4-AD paid RM400 on the 28th, was refunded on the 29th, then came back the same day, paid again and collected. Net of the three steps it is RM400 in and 5 unit out, so it counts everywhere now. All three steps are kept in the trail rather than tidied into one payment, because the refund is the only record that the desk once wrote a price under its own walk-away and nearly lost the sale over it. An advance to the associate, CS6-BS 1 unit at RM110 with nothing paid, so RM110 joins receivables inside his 2 unit cap. A cash sale to CR3-DAM, 1 unit at RM80, paid and collected the same day, and that price is the one to look at: RM80 is below the RM85 walk-away and RM50 under the RM130 the board quoted, which makes it the first order since the 08 Jul package to breach the line outright. He has been the steadiest repeat buyer at about RM85, so it is an established discount rather than a concession, and that is what makes it worth pricing against. And a pending order, 5 unit at RM435, exactly the board, which counts nowhere until money or salt moves. He arrived on a provisional code and was named the same day, so the desk re-keyed him to CZ4-TBC and purged the placeholder. Revenue rises to RM10,937 and margin to RM3,822 at 34.9%; stock falls to 91.6 unit. Shrinkage is unchanged at 26.05 unit, which is the point of rolling the stated count down by the 7 unit delivered rather than leaving it: had it stayed at 98.6 those seven units would have booked as loss. Cover drops from 34.1 days to 26.9 because the fortnight shipping rate rose with them. Second, the five tiers are now the policy. The tab computed its own board while the cards were solved separately, and the two disagreed at nearly every size: RM130 against RM120 at a unit, RM255 against RM270 at 2.5, RM435 against RM460 at five. What he hands a customer was not what the desk said, so one of them had to give and he chose the cards, because they are the thing already sent. SS/S/R/M/P are now the quote board, and the engine keeps the job it is actually good at: the effective cost, the walk-away and the 25%/2% band floors are still computed live, and every tier cell is tested against them. Where a tier prices under the floor the desk says so. Computed live and independently, it reproduces the card notes to the sen: SS is RM3.92 light at a unit and RM39.81 light at 2.5, S clears until RM1.77 light at 3 unit and RM25.70 at 4, and R, M and P clear everywhere they run. That is left visible on purpose, because SS carries no delivery in its cash and earns on its own basis; the floor is the stricter forward-looking test and silencing it to make a card look clean is the one thing not to do. Sizes above 6.25 unit have no card and stay on the engine, shown apart so it is never unclear which is speaking. The reseller menu follows the R card too, since R is the only card that leaves his phone and a published list that disagrees with the card in the customer’s hand is worse than no list. One defect that caught itself: filling 3.5 and 4.5 from the engine put RM97.14 a unit next to RM97.50, so the rate ROSE with size and the ladder inverted. Sizes the R card skips are now dropped rather than filled, because a price list that gets dearer as the lot grows invites one question with no good answer. Third, Customers is reordered around the reading. It used to open with a sortable ledger of every buyer and put the interpretation underneath, so the first thing on screen was raw data and the last thing was what it meant. Now the read leads: how few names carry four-fifths of the book, who sits under a 20% margin, who is late against his own median gap rather than a desk average, and what the overdue ones are worth if the usual lot went out at today’s price. Three charts carry the shape — a Pareto with the cumulative share running across, a bubble chart separating big from profitable with the 20% line drawn, and a diverging bar of who is overdue. The raw table is still there, sortable on every column, at the foot under The database, which is where you go to look a name up rather than to be told something.

The downloaded menu now needs no wifi and opens with a password that stops working (30 Jul). Yesterday’s download traded the expiry away to work offline. This gets it back, and states precisely which half of it is real. The prices are now ciphertext inside the file. AES-GCM under a key derived from the password by PBKDF2-SHA256 at 150,000 iterations, the same scheme and the same count as this desk’s own name vault, so there is one cryptographic idea in the building rather than two. The password is not stored in the file and there is nothing in it to compare against: a wrong password fails because the authentication tag does not verify, not because a check said no. A forwarded file on its own is ciphertext, and that is real protection rather than an assertion. The expiry is authenticated, not merely written down. It is passed as AES-GCM additional authenticated data, so editing the date in the file makes the entire payload refuse to decrypt: tested by extending it, which breaks it. But the comparison is against the reader’s own clock, and a clock can be set backwards, so that half is not proof against a determined reader. The page says so; so does the tab. Overclaiming here would be worse than the gap. And once the password is in, the prices are on a screen, which nothing can un-see, so the code stays tiled across the sheet and a leaked screenshot still names who opened it. A six-character password is generated for each issue, drawn from an alphabet with no O/0 and no I/1/l so it can be read down a phone line, and the tab tells him to send it by a different channel than the file, because the two travelling together makes the lock decoration. Verified end to end: right password renders fifteen lots, wrong password refuses, a backdated file reads as expired, and a tampered expiry will not open. The QR route is unchanged and remains the stricter one, since it keeps the prices out of the file entirely and can be withdrawn.

Today stops repeating Overview, and gets two pictures (30 Jul). He read the tab as haywire next to Forward, and both halves of that were fair. The repetition was measurable and it was one bug, not a style. The rule row built its body by printing every breach in full, `what` and `why` together, which is the same prose the Boundaries table on Overview already carries. One man breaking four rules therefore put four paragraphs on the tab meant to be skimmed: nineteen seven-word phrases on Today appeared word for word on Overview. That is now zero. The row names the rules as chips, states his position once with duplicates removed, and the button goes to Boundaries for the argument. A tab you skim and a tab you study are different jobs, and the desk was doing both in one place. Today was also the only tab with no picture at all, which is exactly why it read as a wall. It now opens with two, both of them the same data as the list rather than anything new: where the money at stake sits, by kind, as a horizontal bar, which answers what sort of problem today is in a way a ranked list cannot; and cover against the trigger in days, putting the one figure that warns before a loss next to the line it is measured on. Items carrying no figure stay off the chart and read as a dash on the list, as they always have. Every row now also carries a hairline bar showing its share of the largest item, drawn in pure CSS rather than Chart.js, so the ranking survives the chart library failing to load, which the charts themselves cannot. No figure moved.

The reseller menu is rebuilt, republished, and can now be downloaded as a page (30 Jul). First, the served page was missing. menu.html had gone from the folder, so `serve_menu.py` was answering every scanned code with a bare 404 and no reseller could see a price. It is rebuilt in the price-card palette, so the menu and the cards he sends now look like one family. The shell still carries no prices: it reads the code off its own URL, asks the server, and the server checks the signature, the expiry and the revocation list before handing anything back. A copy saved out of a browser is an empty shell, which is exactly what makes the QR route perishable. Second, a real bug in that handshake. The success path returned the price payload without an `ok` flag while every refusal returned `ok:false`, so a page testing for a truthy `ok` rejected every valid link. Both halves are fixed: the server now states success explicitly, and the page tests for an explicit false and the status code rather than for truthiness. Third, the published list was stale and wrong. It still held the pre-adjustment prices, RM140 at 1 unit against a board quoting RM130, because it had never picked up the -7% live adjustment. Rather than hand-write a figure the board does not stand behind, the desk’s own `mnRows()` was run to produce exactly what the Publish button sends, and that is what is now in `menu_prices.json`: fifteen lots, RM75 to RM1,610, every one a multiple of five with the rate falling as the lot grows. The old list is kept as a `.v160.bak`. Fourth, Download a page. A new button saves a single self-contained file with the prices inside it, no script, no external reference and nothing to fetch, so it opens on any phone with no server and no wifi. What it gives up is the expiry, and that is stated on the tab rather than buried: a file cannot be withdrawn once sent, so the protection that survives is attribution. The reseller’s code is tiled across the sheet as a repeating SVG background and stamped with the issuing hour, so a leaked file still names who was given it. It uses `codeOf()` and never `ID()`, because `ID()` returns the real name whenever the vault happens to be unlocked and this file leaves the desk.

Quantities are now stated in units, and the folder is filed by function (30 Jul). Two changes, neither of which moves a figure. First, the old mass symbol is gone from every surface. Quantities read 98.6 unit, rates read RM47.47/unit, and the prose no longer names the old unit or its spelled-out form anywhere. The central formatter was changed once, at the single line that appends the suffix, so the board, the ledger, the walk, the charts and every card inherit it rather than each carrying its own label. What did NOT change is the point: the ledger’s quantity field keeps its original name, the queue still posts that same name, and every identifier carrying a quantity is untouched. The unit is a display label, nothing more; renaming the data would have desynchronised this desk from salt_queue.json and from every entry already written. One local variable in the band aggregator shared that name and was renamed first, because a blind pass had turned a rate division into a division by nothing and took the Pricing tab out entirely. That is the whole risk in a rename of this kind, and it is why the test is the rendered page rather than the source. Verified by rendering all sixteen tabs and comparing every number: 5,444 figures, identical before and after, with quote-board invariants holding at RM40, 44, 48 and 56. Second, the project folder is now filed by function: 01_Dashboard holds the desk, deskctl, both servers, the launcher and assets; 02_Reports the finished reports; 03_PriceCards the generated images; 04_Docs the README and instruction notes; 05_Pricing the card and ladder generators; 06_Data everything the servers write. The master is therefore 01_Dashboard/salt_command.html from now on. serve_desk.py and serve_menu.py now write and read through a single DATA constant pointing at 06_Data, so the queue, the vault, the menu prices and the menu secret all sit apart from the code that touches them. DESK.json states both paths explicitly rather than letting any surface guess after the move, and the launcher needed no change because it has always served its own directory. Third, the 100 unit tier on the live quote is corrected from RM4,800 to RM4,700, the rate actually paid and received on 28 Jul. The quote had been carrying a price he had already beaten, which made the top tier read RM48/unit when RM47 was banked. It now shows a RM1/unit discount against the 50 unit tier rather than none. One stale sentence came out with it: the Financials cash line hardcoded the RM4,800 figure and would have gone on saying the P1 buy was RM455 short of covered when the true gap is RM355. It now reads the largest tier off the quote itself, so the two cannot drift apart again. Nothing else moved: the dearest live tier is still the 12.5 unit at RM56, so replacement cost, effective cost and every quote on the board are untouched.

A reseller price list for a phone, opened by QR, live, and reachable only from this wifi (29 Jul). The board on the Pricing tab now publishes to menu.html, a mobile page carrying quantity, price, price per unit, the version and the date. Start with what it cannot do: no web page on any platform can blank a screenshot. There is no iOS Safari API for it, no CSS trick and no header; native Android has FLAG_SECURE and the web has no equivalent, so anything sold as screenshot-proof is theatre. What is built instead makes a leak traceable and perishable. Every page is watermarked with the reseller’s own code and the issue time, tiled across it, so a screenshot names whoever took it. Every link is signed server-side with HMAC-SHA256 over the reseller and the expiry, so nobody can extend a date or mint a link for a code never issued. Every link expires, and can be revoked sooner. And the prices are never in the page: the HTML is an empty shell and the figures arrive only after the server has checked the token, so a saved copy or a look at the source is worth nothing. Verified against a tampered expiry, a forged reseller, an expired link and a missing token, which return 403, 403, 410 and 400, and the shell carries no figure. The menu runs as its own server on its own port, and that is the point: reaching a phone means listening on the wifi, and opening the DESK to the wifi would put /queue and /vault on the network with it. serve_menu.py is read-only and serves three routes; the desk stays on loopback. Live means live: the page re-asks every 45 seconds, so publishing new prices updates a code already sitting in a reseller’s phone without it being scanned again. Three faults found in the building. A hand-written QR encoder was checked matrix-for-matrix against segno and its format bits were wrong, so it was thrown away and segno vendored into assets instead; a code that does not scan is worth less than no code. The port in every QR came out as the desk’s 8766, because the menu module read argv at import time and argv belonged to the desk. And the LAN address came out as 100.100.39.246, a NordLynx tunnel in the 100.64/10 carrier-grade NAT range that no phone on the wifi could ever reach, because the usual trick of opening a socket towards 8.8.8.8 returns whatever the default route uses, and the default route was the VPN. Addresses are now gathered from every interface, scored, and tunnel ranges excluded, with SALT_LAN_IP to override.

Two finished plans were still shouting on the Today list (29 Jul). P1, the 100 unit buy, and P13, the Monday-orders-Tuesday-stock gap, were both marked committed and both past their date, so Today ranked them under Now alongside a live debt and a banned buyer. Both had in fact been settled by the 28 Jul receipt: P1 bought at RM47/unit for RM4,700, and P13 closed because the restock landed before anything had to be deferred. They are now done, with the outcome written onto each rather than the plan simply vanishing, since what a plan actually led to is the only part worth keeping. Now drops from seven items to five, and the two that remain against a date are real: the SF6-KLC recoverable and P15, the capital reduction, which is still an open decision. A list stops being read the moment it carries things that are already done, which is the same reason four rules about one man were grouped into one row at v147. Nothing else moves: no figure on the desk is derived from a plan.

Every sale now carries the cost of the salt that actually went out, and margin falls three points (29 Jul). Twenty priced orders carried no lot cost and fell back to wavgBuy, the flat RM51.72 average over everything ever received. That average now contains the 14 Jul RM48 lot and the 28 Jul RM47 lot, so it was back-dating cheap salt onto June sales that could only have come off RM64 stock. Each of the twenty is now stated. The costs are derived, not guessed. Lots are queued in receipt order through the desk’s own poRecvKg, so the defaulted RM60 lot never enters the queue, and deliveries are consumed in delivery-date order. Where a row already stated a cost, that cost is kept and consumed from the matching lot, because those were specific identifications rather than FIFO: the 14 Jul sales at RM48 came out of the 50 unit lot that landed the same day, which no first-in rule would have given them. The walk reconciles at both ends: 236.15 unit in including opening, 111.50 unit delivered, 124.65 unit left, which is the counted 98.60 plus the 26.05 unit plug, to the unit. Cost of goods rises RM308.03 and gross margin falls from RM3,868.74 to RM3,560.71, from 37.39% to 34.41%. Revenue, collections, stock, cash and every receivable are untouched; this moves the cost side and nothing else. The flattering was almost entirely retail. Profit per unit on lot cost falls from RM49.32 to RM42.83 at 1 unit and under, and from RM43.73 to RM38.56 between 1 and 6.25 unit. Above 6.25 unit it does not move by a sen, because all six of those lots already carried a stated cost. The band that read worst was the only one that had been telling the truth. STOCK_COST is deliberately left at RM47.47. A pure first-in remnant reads RM47.02, but reaching it means attributing the undated shrinkage plug to particular lots, which v157 declined to do on the ground that it would be an invention. That reasoning has not changed and this does not reopen it. Two rows still carry no cost and should not: the 20 Jul CC5-OKR order was cancelled before anything moved, and the 28 Jul CA5-KER unit is pending. One thing was examined and not built: a self-funding wholesale floor, set so that two or three 12.5 unit lots would pay for the next one. At the live effective cost that is RM1,050 to RM1,185 against a board of RM870. It was dropped once the trade record showed that only two of the eight lots ever sold at or above 5 unit would have cleared it, and those eight lots are 81.75 unit of the book. The finding worth keeping is that there is no trade anywhere between RM82.86 and RM104.00/unit, so any floor in that range refuses exactly the same six lots.

The 5 unit sale unwound, the new buyer is named, and the first fresh count since the lot landed is 2.72 unit light (29 Jul). Three queued entries, and the first two are the same event. The RM400 came back. The buyer who paid in full on the 28th and never collected was refunded in full on the 29th, so the order has nothing paid against it and nothing delivered, which by the desk’s own rule makes it PENDING and counts nowhere. It leaves revenue, it leaves collected cash, and the 5 unit it was holding comes off deferred and back into free-to-sell. The order is not deleted, because an order that unwound is a fact about the book and deleting it would lose the only record that the desk once wrote a price RM15 under its own walk-away. It sits in the Order book with the reasoning intact. The buyer is named, so the provisional code is re-keyed to CE4-AD and the placeholder is purged from the transactions and the roster, per the standing one-identifier rule. Two changelog mentions of the placeholder survive on purpose, exactly as v148 decided: they describe the format the generator produces rather than naming a party, and purging them would leave the record of the mechanism factually wrong. The encrypted vault cannot be re-keyed from here, since it opens only on your passphrase, so the name needs typing once against CE4-AD in Names and IDs. And the count. 98.6 unit counted by hand against a roll of 101.32, so 2.72 unit is unaccounted for and books as shrinkage, because the count always wins. That is the first physical count since the 100 unit landed, and the direction is the opposite of what the raw units suggest. The plug rises 2.72 unit to 26.05 unit, but it is measured against everything ever handled, and that denominator already rose 100 unit at v156, so the observed rate goes from 9.88% to 11.03% and the effective cost the board prices off is RM62.94/unit. Against the new lot on its own the loss is 2.72%, comfortably inside the 7.5% the buy simulator assumes, which is the first hard evidence that the old 17.14% carried early handling mistakes rather than a standing rate. One count is not a trend: 2.72 unit could be moisture, weighing tolerance on receipt, or handling, and the desk cannot tell which from a single count. A second count is what would turn this into a rate, and until there is one the desk reports the number rather than explaining it away. STOCK_COST is left at RM47.47, since the shelf is still the same two lots and attributing the missing 2.72 unit to one of them rather than the other would be an invention; on either attribution the blended rate moves by about two sen.

The 100 unit landed, and the shelf goes from a third of a day of cover to a fortnight (28 Jul). Three entries. The 100 unit from SA5-BTR is paid in full and received in full at RM4,700, held to the price he first offered rather than the RM4,800 he later quoted, so plan P1 is closed and the cheapest rate the desk has ever paid is on the shelf. Bought to date rises to 231.25 unit and the weighted average falls from RM55.19 to RM51.72. CA4-DAM took his 1.5 unit, agreed on the 26th and paid and delivered on the 28th once the lot arrived, RM175 at RM116.67/unit, his fourth order and his largest. And a new buyer paid RM400 for 5 unit and has not taken it, so the salt is owed out: it sits on the shelf, comes off free-to-sell, and shows as deferred. He is on a provisional code until he is named. Stock is rolled to 101.32 unit, free to sell 95.07 against 6.25 unit owed out, and cover moves from 0.3 days to 15.9. Cash falls from RM8,950 to RM4,825. Revenue reaches RM10,747 and margin RM4,034 at 37.5%. The desk is no longer short of its own promises, the first time in this record. Read the shrinkage figure carefully. It now reports 9.9%, down from 17.1%, and nothing has improved: the plug is still exactly 23.33 unit, spread over a base that grew by 100 unit. Effective cost falls to RM62.14 as a consequence, which flatters every margin on the board. The rate will only mean something once a lot is weighed in and out; until then a big purchase makes the leak look smaller than it is. Two faults fixed in the same pass. Cash was dated by the ORDER date, so CA4-DAM’s payment made on the 28th would have been filed under the 26th and swallowed by the 28 Jul cash count instead of landing after it; it now follows paidOn where a row carries one, exactly as delivery follows deliveredOn. And a count is now read as at the start of its date rather than the end, so money moved later the same day accrues on top of it rather than vanishing into it. One thing to look at. The 5 unit at RM80/unit is under the board’s own walk-away of RM415 for that size, by RM15. It still earns RM33/unit against the RM47 lot it came off, but only RM17.86 against what the next unit costs to replace.

The clock was being composed rather than read, and deskctl now refuses to let that pass (28 Jul). Every stamp in the v147 to v154 run was written as a plausible-looking progression of times, forty to eighty minutes apart, instead of being read off the machine. It looked entirely convincing and it rolled past a midnight that had not happened: v153 and v154 were stamped 29 Jul, 2.6 hours into the future. A stamp is a figure like any other and the desk’s own first rule is that figures are not invented. LAST_UPDATED is now set from the clock and the two prose dates that had drifted to 29 Jul are corrected. The earlier stamps in that run are approximate and are left as they stand rather than replaced with a second set of guesses; the version order is what carries the sequence, and it is sound. deskctl.py stamp now parses LAST_UPDATED and compares it to the real clock, warning and exiting non-zero when it is in the future or more than a day and a half stale, so the next time it happens the tool says so instead of the reader having to notice. Two other corrections in the same pass. The mirror comparison was byte-for-byte, which was wrong: publishing joins the DOCTYPE and the artifact meta tag onto one line, so a successful push always came back as a difference. A checker that cries wolf every time is worse than none, because it teaches you to ignore it. The comparison is now the hash of the desk’s own inline script payload, which no wrapper rewrite can move and no real divergence can hide from. Verified against the live mirror: identical content, one byte of wrapper apart, so the v154 push had in fact succeeded. And the two file paths are now resolved from SALT_MASTER and SALT_MIRROR, then a paths block in DESK.json, then the defaults, so the same command works from Windows and from a mounted sandbox rather than only from the one layout it was written on.

Two copies of this desk existed and nothing said which one was current (28 Jul). The master in the project folder had reached v153 while the published mirror in Artifacts sat at v146, seven versions and two days behind, because everything that day was built in Claude Code, which has no update_artifact and so cannot publish. Nothing anywhere reported the gap. The rule that should have caught it existed, in the daily task’s own instructions, and did not, because a rule has to be remembered. The rule is now mechanical. deskctl.py answers in one command, from either surface: master version, mirror version, both hashes, and exactly what is out of step, exiting non-zero so it fails loudly rather than politely. status is the mandatory first action of any session; check parses the script with node; stamp records the master after a version bump; published records the mirror after a Cowork push. DESK.json holds the record between sessions.
