It also names the direction of travel, which was the thing genuinely never written down: the project-folder file is the only master, and the artefact is a publish target that is never a source, never hand-edited, and never the base for a session even when it looks newer. If the mirror is ever ahead, that means something published without updating the master, and status says stop and reconcile by hand rather than guessing. And the desk now says which copy you are looking at. A badge in the header reads master, writes to disk or mirror, read only. It decides from the queue ping rather than from the URL, because the ping is the thing that actually proves write access and a URL can lie about it. Anything typed into a mirror is lost the moment the master is republished over it, and that is now visible before you type rather than after.

The agreed 100 unit was reading as Open and Deferred in the Ledger, and fixing it uncovered three more (28 Jul). The reported fault. ledgerBuy worked out what a lot had been paid with a bare fallback, an absent cash field meant paid in full, so the agreed 100 unit came back Paid and Undelivered and fell through to Open · Deferred, which reads as salt owed to you against money already handed over. It now reads Pending. This is the fifth site in the v146 family and it was missed in the v147 sweep, which looked at aggregations and not at the state labels. poCash is hardened and is now the single answer to what a lot has been paid: pending pays nothing, an explicit figure always wins, and only a row that actually says paid is assumed paid, where before any row without a cash field was. Two other sites that were correct only because their status field happened to read the right way now go through it too. A worse one next door. Paying or receiving against an agreed-only lot through the queue never cleared the pending flag, so poCash and poRecvKg would have kept returning zero for it by design: the payment you had just recorded and the units you had just taken in would both have vanished from every figure, and the row would have sat pending for ever. It clears now. And the fix for that one opened the original wound, which the test caught before it shipped. poRecvKg treats a lot with no receivedQty as FULLY RECEIVED, which is how every historical lot is booked, so simply clearing the flag walked all 100 unit into stock and the cost basis the moment a deposit was paid: buyKg 231.25, weighted average down to RM51.72, on salt still sitting in a warehouse. Clearing pending now states the receipt explicitly, nothing received and the lot on order. Verified across four paths: a deposit with nothing received, paid in full with nothing received, paid with half received, and paid and received in full. Only the last completes; the first two move cash and leave stock alone. One inconsistency found while testing: the buy simulator computed its new weighted cost off purchases alone while the desk computes wavgBuy with the opening stock folded in, so it was comparing RM55.19 against RM51.46 on two different bases and part of the saving it showed was the mismatch. Both are now on the same basis.

Shrinkage stops being prorated, and the buy simulator stops giving the wrong answer because of it (28 Jul). The desk had one assumption welded in everywhere: that shrinkage is a RATE, so a lot twice the size loses twice the salt. The trader has corrected it. The recorded 17.1% is not what the next lot will lose, because the plug carries early mistakes that are not expected to repeat, and the expectation is 7.5% and then 5%. Three named levels now drive the buy simulator, each traceable rather than derived: observed from the record, expected 7.5% and settled 5% from the trader, with expected as the default, because pricing a new purchase off a problem being fixed builds the problem into the price. Effective cost on a lot is now computed from what survives rather than from a rate, so it is right whichever model applies, and the board comparison is re-labelled effective against effective instead of headline against effective, which was not like for like. One thing was built and then removed as an invented figure. A fixed loss per restock was first derived by dividing the 23.33 unit plug by nine received lots, giving 2.59 unit, which works out at 2.6% on a 100 unit lot: lower than the 5% the trader expects at the very end of the journey, and produced entirely by a denominator chosen by the desk rather than measured on the shelf. It is gone. SHRINK.cycleKg is left null and documented, so the fixed model becomes available the moment a real per-restock loss is weighed, and not before. A trajectory table on Pricing now runs the three bands at each shrinkage level with selling prices held at what each has actually realised, so only the cost moves. It settles the question the cap decision turns on. At RM56 buying, bulk goes from minus RM0.27 a unit at 17.1%, to RM6.74 at 7.5%, to RM8.33 at 5%, so wholesale stops losing money somewhere before the near-term target. But the column that matters does not move at all: small packs less bulk is RM35.19 a unit at every level. A cost improvement subtracts the same ringgit from every band and lifts them together, so it can make wholesale viable and can never make it competitive. Whether wholesale is worth doing is a cost question and both cheaper salt and less shrinkage answer it yes; whether it is the best use of a unit is a price question, and nothing on the cost side touches it.

Profit per unit, and the answer on wholesale is no (28 Jul). Margin as a percentage flatters a big lot: 10% of a RM935 order sounds survivable until you see it is RM7 a unit against RM35 on a half. Ringgit per unit is the figure that decides which trade is worth doing, because a unit is what this desk keeps running out of, not customers. Two new sections on Pricing. What each size earns gives profit per unit across the board and then the same figure for every order actually written, split into three bands and measured two ways. Lot cost is what that salt really cost and judges a trade already done; replacement cost is what the next unit costs with shrinkage carried and is the only basis for doing it again. A trade can be fine on the first and a loss on the second, and here several are. The bands read RM34.89 a unit at or under 1 unit, RM28.48 from 1 to 6.25 unit, and RM6.30 above it: a unit in a small pack earns five and a half times a unit in bulk. Wholesale under review puts the verdict in ringgit. Stripping the CM6-HCM one-off, five lots above 6.25 unit moved 57 unit for RM3,835 at RM67.28/unit against a RM67.58 effective cost, a loss of RM17, minus 30 sen a unit. Three of the six large lots sit under replacement cost outright and a fourth clears it by 42 sen. Repricing cannot rescue it: 20% on a 12.5 unit lot needs RM84.48/unit against a median cleared of RM66.40, a 27% rise no buyer but the one-off has ever paid, so this is not a pricing problem the desk can reprice its way out of. But the cause is the shrinkage, not the price. The same 57 unit at the bare RM56 replacement rate earns RM643, RM11.28 a unit. Wholesale carries no margin cushion, so it is the first thing a 17.1% leak destroys, which makes plan P4 worth more to it than any price rise available and makes this decision reversible rather than final. A ladder cap can now be tested from the tab: enter a size and the board marks everything above it as not sold and reports what refusing those orders would have cost and saved. Nothing is committed by testing; SALES_POLICY.maxLot is where a cap becomes policy, and it is deliberately still null. The counterfactual is shown but labelled: those 57 unit at small-pack rates would have earned about RM1,989 if the demand existed, and this desk has never sold that volume in small packs, so it is a ceiling rather than a forecast. Recorded as plan P16. A chart underneath plots profit per unit against lot size with every order laid over it and the replacement cost as the zero line, which is the whole argument in one picture.

Shrinkage was understated by 6 unit, orders now carry a delivery and a payment date, and the shelf reconstructs cleanly (28 Jul). The loan, confirmed and corrected. The 12 May loan of 6 unit was being subtracted from the shelf a second time, and the trader has now confirmed the 4.90 unit counted on 26 Jun was counted AFTER that salt had gone. It therefore never left during the recorded period and must not be deducted again. The correction runs the opposite way to what was first expected: the loan sat on the deduction side, so removing it leaves MORE unaccounted, not less. Self-use and shrinkage rises from 17.33 unit to 23.33 unit, the rate from 12.7% to 17.1%, and the effective cost that every price on the board is measured against from RM64.17 to RM67.58/unit. The desk had been flattering itself. Nothing else moves: revenue is still RM10,172 and margin RM3,655 at 35.9%, because the count always wins and the plug is what absorbs the difference. What does move is judgement: realised margin on the whole book now reads 20.4% against the effective cost rather than 24.4%, bulk reads 9.3%, and a 12.5 unit lot on the board earns 10%. Plan P4 said shrinkage costs more than any pricing decision on the desk, and it is worse than it said. The flag is on the loan record rather than in the formula, so a loan made AFTER a future count still counts in full. Orders now carry deliveredOn and paidOn. Both are derived rather than copied onto every row, in a fixed order of trust: the amendment trail first, then an explicit field added only where a note was the sole record of a date, then the order date marked ASSUMED. Ten orders date from the trail, four from a note that had never been machine-readable (CZ6-WM, the 7 unit to CS6-BS, and the two 23 July deliveries to CA4-DAM and CR4-PJ), and 23 remain assumed. The reconstructed shelf is now clean: it never goes below zero, bottoms at 1.63 unit and still finishes on the counted 2.82 unit, where a day earlier it fell to minus 12.31 unit on nine impossible days. A new panel measures the working capital the desk could previously only describe: order to delivery averages 0.3 days, order to payment 1.8 days with a longest of 27, and five orders let the salt go before the cash arrived, RM967 of it. Assumed dates contribute a zero lag, so those are floors and the true gaps can only be longer. And a tool, after a self-inflicted lesson: a single mismatched quote closed with a backtick took the ENTIRE script down. The page still drew its shell, the console came back empty, and the only symptom was a bare "builders is not defined". check_syntax.py now parses the script out of the file and runs node over it before a browser ever sees it, and maps any error back to a line in the HTML. It costs a second and it catches the one class of fault that hides itself.

Six charts, a map, a planned dividend, and two faults the charts themselves found (28 Jul). The desk had become a wall of figures, so this adds the pictures that carry a decision. Analysis holds six, each answering a question the desk had only ever answered in prose: a bridge from revenue to margin with shrinkage shown beside it rather than inside it, since it is already paid for in the cost of goods and putting it in the bridge would deduct it twice; every priced order as a dot against the live board and the walk-away line, which is plans P2, P3 and P5 in one picture; the shelf rebuilt day by day; revenue by buyer with a cumulative share; every lot ever bought plotted size against rate, with the defaulted one marked; and one row per buyer showing when each actually orders, where the gaps are the point. The stock chart immediately found two things. First, the walk finished 6 unit above every other figure on the desk, because recompute subtracts the 12 May loan from the shelf and the reconstruction did not. Second, and worse, it goes below zero on nine days, which is impossible. That is a dating fault, not a stockout: salt moves when it is handed over, and 27 of 38 delivering orders carry no structured Fulfilment step, so the walk has to fall back to the order date and units leave before the lot that supplied them arrives. The 21 to 23 July stretch is the clearest case, where orders were agreed one day and delivered once the restock landed, with the real date written only in a note. The fix is a field, not a formula, and it is flagged on the tab rather than smoothed away; no total is affected, which is exactly why nothing else had noticed. A map, drawn as a schematic and deliberately not a street map, because these are neighbourhood centroids read off order notes rather than addresses. Only the seven suffixes the ledger itself explains are placed. The other fourteen parties are listed as unplaced and stay that way: SB, BJ, DAM, PER, TAI, CHE, SK, BS, BTR and KER are all guessable and none is written down anywhere, and a pin invented from an abbreviation looks exactly like a pin that was known. Put a suffix in PLACES with a rough latitude and longitude and it appears; give it an exact pair later and set exact:true. The planned capital reduction is on the Whiteboard as P15 and modelled on Forward behind a switch, alongside a second switch for the agreed 100 unit. Neither books anything. On the counted RM8,950 the two together land cash at exactly RM250, drawing RM4,180, and the shelf still empties inside the window with RM437 to restock from, which is the sequencing question P15 asks you to look at before doing it. One design fault fixed, and it was not new: KPI rows set their column count with an inline style, which beats the mobile media query on specificity, so a five-across row stayed five across on a phone and crushed every figure in it. The Pricing tab had carried that since v138. Widths are now classes the media query can override, and all sixteen tabs collapse to two columns on a 375px screen with no horizontal overflow.

Cash is counted rather than guessed, two renames commit, and Today stops shouting (28 Jul). Cash first, because it unlocks the question v147 had to refuse. The opening balance on 26 Jun was never written down, and asking for it would have put a guess underneath every figure downstream. So cash is now counted, exactly as stock already is: you state what you hold on a date and the desk works backwards. Counted at RM8,950 on 28 Jul, and since trading has moved RM1,212 net across the whole book, the opening balance must have been about RM7,738. That is stated as a consequence, never as an input. Recorded trade accrues on top of the count; anything before it is simply inside it. Count again in a month and the gap between what the trade says you should hold and what is actually there becomes visible, which is the cash equivalent of shrinkage and the only way spending that never gets written down ever surfaces. If an opening balance is ever stated as well, the two are compared and the difference is reported rather than reconciled away. The 100 unit is therefore answerable at last: it fits. Free cash is RM8,870 after the RM80 refund owed, the buy takes RM4,700, and the low point over the next thirty days is RM4,430. Two renames committed. The results are CZ6-WM, relocated within Wangsa Maju, and CA5-KER, the provisional code the new buyer arrived on, now graduated. Both retired codes are purged outright from the transactions, the roster, the vault code map and every changelog entry, per the standing rule, which is why this entry names only what they became. One mention was deliberately kept: the v145 entry describing how the generator mints a provisional code still says NEW-1, because that is the format the generator actually produces and purging it would leave the record of the mechanism factually wrong. The encrypted name vault could not be re-keyed here, since it is opened only by your passphrase, so the two names need retyping once against their new codes in Names and IDs. Today, redesigned. The action list was a table, which crushed the reason text into a cell and gave every row the same weight. It is now a list of cards: a severity rail down the left, the kind as a word rather than an emoji (an emoji reads slower, not faster, and dates badly), the money on the right where the eye can run down the column, and room between rows. Three things that said the same thing three times are now one. Being short on promises and being under the reorder trigger were two rows and a banner, but they are one trip to the supplier, so they are one row; the shelf state stays in the headline figures where it belongs. Rules broken by one person were already grouped in v147, and the same discipline now applies across the tab: say it once, in the place that can act on it.

The desk starts looking forward, and three figures it was quietly getting wrong are fixed (28 Jul). Everything here was a rear-view mirror: excellent on what had happened, silent on what to do about it. Four things change. First, three bugs, all one family. v146 taught the desk that a PENDING buy counts nowhere and guarded it at source in poRecvKg, but four things downstream still read the raw row. Cash flow treated the agreed 100 unit as money already spent, because an absent cash field falls back to the full total, so trading net read −RM3,488 when it was +RM1,212, a RM4,700 error on a bank account the lot had never touched. The 30-day buy rate averaged in a lot nobody has paid for and read RM50.74/unit instead of RM53.89, which also put a rate the desk has never achieved on the Pricing tab as a quick-set chip. And Inventory listed the same 100 unit as still to arrive while the Overview correctly showed nothing in transit, so two panels contradicted each other on one page load. A single poCash() and poLive() now answer both questions at source. Second, the Today tab, and the desk now opens on it. Nothing on it is new information: every item was already computed somewhere, but it was scattered over seven tabs and nothing ranked one against another. Severity follows a rule and inside a severity the sort is purely money at stake, so the order can always be explained. Rules broken by one person are grouped into one row rather than four, because four rows about one man is a list you stop reading. The first thing it surfaced had never been stated anywhere: 6.69 unit is promised out against 2.82 unit on the shelf, so the desk is 3.87 unit short of orders already agreed. Promises live in the Order book and salt lives in Inventory, and nothing had ever subtracted one from the other. Third, the Forward tab. Stock and cash on a daily line, built only from what is already on the book: units promised, the observed shipping rate, the desk’s own 10-day credit term and the provisioning ladder. There is no demand model, nothing seasonal and nothing fitted. Two stock lines are drawn rather than one, because committed needs no forecast at all and committed plus rate is an estimate, and merging them would pass the second off as the first. Receivables land net of provisioning, so an old debt contributes what it is realistically worth. Fourth, the Sourcing tab, which answers the live P1 question. Put a quantity and a rate in and it re-runs the cost base, the board and the forward view as though the lot had landed: the agreed 100 unit at RM47 moves the weighted average from RM55.19 to RM51.46, loses about 12.73 unit to shrinkage before a unit sells, and pushes the empty shelf from today out to 14 Aug. Beside it a supplier scorecard, which the desk has never had: share over the last 30 days rather than all time, because a supplier who has stopped supplying still carries his old all-time share, plus units received against units bought, so SF6-KLC reads 67% and the RM750 default is a column rather than a paragraph. It states plan P10 as a figure: SA5-BTR is now 89% of recent sourcing, and the agreed 100 unit would concentrate over six times the exposure that has already burned once. Also, on the Customers tab, who to approach next. Cadence is the median gap between a customer’s own order dates, so it is a habit he has actually shown rather than a desk average applied to him; a customer with one order is left blank rather than given someone else’s. It reads that CG5-SB is 23 days past his own four-day habit, and that CR3-DAM has been paying RM85/unit against a board that now asks 71% more, which is the per-customer version of plans P2 and P5. Nothing on any of the three new tabs books anything, and the affordability of the 100 unit still cannot be answered, because OPENING_CASH remains unset: the desk knows the buy costs RM4,700 and refuses to pretend it knows whether the money is there.

Four queued entries committed, one rename held back, and a pending buy that would have moved every margin on the desk (27 Jul). The first run through the new rename machinery, and it worked, though it also exposed two faults worth more than the entries themselves. Committed. Two renames applied and the old codes purged outright, from the transactions, the roster and every changelog entry: CN6-WM and CZ6-WM, both relocated to Wangsa Maju. The 100 unit buy from plan P1 is recorded against SA5-BTR at RM4,700, RM47/unit, agreed with nothing paid and nothing received. And a new buyer took 1 unit at RM120, also agreed only. Both are pending, so they count nowhere. The pending buy nearly did real damage. A lot with no explicit received quantity was taken as fully received, which is how every historical lot was booked, so the 100 unit walked straight into stock and the cost basis: bought-to-date read 231.25 unit, the weighted average fell to RM51.46, and because untagged sales cost out at that average, margin rose to RM3,764 on trade that had not happened. A pending buy now reports zero received at source, and is excluded from payables and from in-transit besides. Figures are back where they belong: revenue RM10,172, margin RM3,655 at 35.9%, bought to date 131.25 unit at RM54.86, weighted average RM55.19. The Order book’s supplier pending section, empty since it was built, now holds its first row. One rename was NOT applied. The queue asked to pull the general bucket out to a numbered end customer. That is the v144 test failing: the code generator still derived a code from a name alone, when the rule is a name and a place, so it offered a button it should never have offered. The generator is fixed rather than the symptom: a reseller’s end buyer with no location keeps his bucket and no rename is offered, and the bucket no longer consumes a number, so buyers either side of it cannot be renumbered by it. Verified: the two located buyers hold their numbers unchanged, and a provisional code with both a name and a place graduates cleanly. Add a location to that buyer and the rename will offer itself properly. CA5-KER is live, the first provisional code the desk has minted, sitting in the ledger with no name against it exactly as intended.

One identifier per party, and a name is typed once (27 Jul). The desk asked for a name when you recorded a transaction only so it could mint a code, then threw the name away, because a name is stored only when you separately unlock Names and IDs and save. So every name was typed twice and the first typing was discarded. Worse, that first typing travelled into salt_queue.json, which is plaintext, so the one file that was never meant to hold a name was quietly collecting them. Three changes end it. 1. The Transaction form no longer asks for a name. Choosing "add new" now mints a provisional code, NEW-1, and books the order against that. No name field, so nothing to type twice and nothing to leak. 2. Naming happens once, in Names and IDs, and the re-key is queued from there. When a name implies a code different from the one the ledger carries, the panel no longer just nags about it: it offers the rename as a button, which puts a rename entry on the queue carrying only the two codes, never the name. I apply it on the next run, re-keying every transaction and purging the old code outright. Three guards refuse the ways it could go wrong: renaming onto a code another party already holds, queueing the same party twice, and a rename to itself. 3. Nothing changes on screen until the re-key is applied. That is the whole point, and it is worth stating plainly because the tempting design is the opposite one. A stable internal key with a prettier code painted over it was considered and rejected: the moment the ledger says one thing and the screen says another, you are back to two identifiers for one party, which is the double work rather than the cure. So the id in the data and the code on the screen are the same string, always, and the price of that is a queued re-key rather than an instant relabel. A small thing that matters for provisional codes: a row in Names and IDs with no name against it is unidentifiable, so each unnamed party now shows the trade it arrived on, first seen date, weight and value, read off the ledger. You will know who CA5-KER was. No figure moves: revenue RM10,172, margin RM3,655, receivables RM333 net, stock 2.82 unit.

A name alone no longer earns a code; it takes a name and a place (27 Jul). The test is corrected. A reseller’s end buyer was pulled out of the general bucket at v141 on the reasoning that a name in the vault meant he was no longer unknown. That was the wrong test. The rule you actually work to is that a buyer earns his own code when you know who he is and where he is, because a location is what proves you dealt with him yourself rather than merely heard a name. Two transactions move back to the bucket, the 17 Jul unit at RM115 and the 21 Jul 7 unit at RM580, and both now sit under CS6-BS-Gen, which becomes a live code with real trade behind it. The code minted at v141 is purged outright, from the roster, from both sale notes and from all three changelog entries that named it, leaving no translation table behind. The two who keep their codes keep them for the right reason, not because they were named first: CS6-BS-1-MK at Mont Kiara and CS6-BS-2-BK at Bandar Kinrara both carry a place, because you delivered to both. No figure moves: the salt, the money and the reseller attribution are identical whichever label the end buyer carries. Revenue RM10,172, margin RM3,655 at 35.9%, receivables RM333 net, stock 2.82 unit. What changes is that his end-customer count now reads two known buyers plus one bucket, which is the honest shape of what you know. One thing you have to do yourself: the vault still holds a name under the purged code, and I cannot edit an encrypted blob. Unlock Names and IDs, clear that entry and press Save, and the desk and the vault agree again.

The general downsell bucket is renamed, and the dead codes are gone for good (27 Jul). 1. <reseller>-X becomes <reseller>-Gen. When a reseller sells on to someone you never meet, the sale books to that reseller’s single general bucket, and that bucket is now written CS6-BS-Gen rather than a bare letter. The mechanism is untouched, only the label: one bucket per reseller, never a fresh code per stranger, so his own buying still reads apart from what he moves onward. Gen says what it is, a general downsell customer whose name is not known, where X read like a placeholder someone had forgotten to fill in, which is precisely the wrong signal for a code that is meant to be a permanent answer rather than a gap. The bucket is currently empty, so nothing is re-keyed and no row, roster entry or figure moves: revenue RM10,172, margin RM3,655, receivables RM333 net and stock 2.82 unit all stand. A -Gen code comes into existence the first time it is used and is never seeded onto the roster empty, because a code with no trade behind it is exactly the kind of reference this desk has just finished removing. 2. Superseded codes are purged outright. The one-convention rule had left two dead codes alive in a translation table, on the reasoning that a future reader might meet them in an old note. That reasoning is now rejected: a purge with an exception is not a purge, and a translation table is itself a live reference to something that does not exist. Both are struck from this file entirely, including from the v141 entry that recorded them and from the split-rule comment that used one as an illustration. Those passages now describe what happened without naming what no longer is. 3. Consistent wording. The two sale notes, the Transaction tab dropdown and its helper line all said “unknown bucket” while the code said -X; all four now say general bucket and show the -Gen form, so the thing is called one name in the code, on the screen and in the notes.

The desk reads the date off the clock now (27 Jul). TODAY was a hard-coded constant, so ageing, provisioning, cover and the demand windows all froze at whatever date the last push stamped. A file opened three days later still aged every debt to the day it was written, which is the one kind of staleness a desk cannot afford, because provisioning is supposed to get worse on its own. It is now taken from the clock at each load, in KL time: the instant is shifted by eight hours before the calendar day is read, so a morning before 08:00 KL is not booked back to the previous UTC day, and the day is parsed back to midnight so every age stays a whole number of days rather than a fraction. Nothing is re-stated. Rolling from 26 to 27 July moves no provisioning band and no figure: revenue RM10,172, margin RM3,655 at 35.9%, trade receivables RM490 gross and RM333 net, the SF6-KLC recoverable RM188 net, stock 2.82 unit and free to sell 1.57 unit all read exactly as they did. What changes is that they keep reading correctly without a push. Two steps now arrive on their own. CS6-PER passes 14 days on 28 Jul and provisions to 75%, taking net trade receivables from RM333 to RM260; the SF6-KLC recoverable reaches 21 days on 29 Jul and provisions in full, taking RM188 to nil. Neither needs anyone to remember. The caveat worth knowing. Two figures here are counted rather than derived, the shelf at 2.82 unit and the shrinkage plug at 17.33 unit, and a clock cannot age either. So this file opened weeks from now will age its debts honestly and still show a stale shelf, and the cover reading will decay as the fortnight window slides past the last recorded sale. The count still has to come from you.

Two codes re-keyed to match the vault (26 Jul). The Names and IDs panel reported that two names implied a different code from the one the ledger carried, and both were aligned. CE4-CHE: the code is derived from the name, the name in the vault changed shape, so the code followed it. A reseller’s end buyer was also numbered out of the general bucket, on the reasoning that a name in the vault meant he was no longer unknown. That reasoning was reversed at v144, which put him back in the bucket, so the code minted here no longer exists. Per the one-convention rule the superseded codes are purged from every transaction, from the roster, from the vault and from every changelog entry including this one, so nothing anywhere in this file still carries them and a future reader cannot mistake either for a separate party. Two things did not change. The bucket survives as a mechanism: it is empty again, and the next stranger a reseller sells to mints a fresh one. And no figure moves, because a code is a label on a party and not a term of any trade: revenue RM10,172, margin RM3,655, receivables RM333 net and stock 2.82 unit all read as they did before the re-key. The two sale notes that described that buyer as unknown are rewritten to say when and why he stopped being so.

Two standings end, one seat opens, and an outlier is named (26 Jul). No existing figure moves: revenue RM10,172, margin RM3,655, receivables RM333 net, stock 2.82 unit. CS6-PER is permanently banned from sale and off the associate bench. The ledger is not rewritten to suit the decision: he genuinely did introduce CH6-TBC and that row stands. What ends is what he may do next. The ban is a breach row of its own, the Transaction tab now refuses a new sale to him rather than merely warning, and the RM290 stays live, aged, provisioned and pursued, with payments still recordable as an amendment to his existing order. A ban ends the trade, not the debt. CJ4-OKR has departed for personal reasons and is memorialised as Co-Founder, a title held by him alone and not passed on. He stays on the tree, because RM2,090 brought in across five customers against RM80 ever spent is earned history rather than a live relationship. The work he did in substance is now the named position of Chief Business Development Officer, and it is recorded as vacant rather than quietly absorbed, so filling it has to be a decision someone takes. CM6-HCM is marked a one-off on the trader’s own reading. It is not removed, because the money was real, but the Pricing tab now carries a second wholesale line with one-offs stripped, and the difference is the point: wholesale reads RM74.51/unit at 13.9% with it and RM68.40/unit at 6.2% without. The desk is marked to price off the stripped figure. Recorded: a pending order, CA4-DAM 1.5 unit at RM175, which counts nowhere until something moves. Whiteboard: P13 on the large order trickling in from Monday against a Tuesday restock, with 1.57 unit of cover in between, and P14 on the two standing changes and the vacant seat.

One price policy, anchored to what the desk actually commands (26 Jul). There were two margin systems and they disagreed: a size-banded floor of 45/40/37.5% driving Boundaries and the Transaction check, and a separate 65-to-40% log taper driving the quote board. The Transaction tab could pass a price the Pricing tab called below floor. Both are gone, replaced by one policy that every part of the desk now reads. It is anchored to two prices given by the trader rather than to a curve chosen for its shape: retail 6.25 unit at RM550 (RM88/unit) and wholesale 12.5 unit at RM875 (RM70/unit), with a hard RM825 money floor on the 12.5 unit lot that no signal, party overlay or rounding can go under. Between the two anchors the per-unit price falls as a power curve, which is a cliff rather than a taper, because wholesale is a different trade and not merely a larger retail order. Floors now differ by band, deliberately. Retail holds 25%; wholesale holds 2%. That is not a concession, it is arithmetic: RM825 for 12.5 unit is 2.8% once the 12.7% shrinkage load is carried, so a single 30% floor would have refused every wholesale order this desk has ever written, which is precisely how a floor gets ignored. The board now reads RM90 at 0.5 unit, RM150 at 1 unit, RM595 at 6.25 unit, RM945 at 12.5 unit and RM1,765 at 25 unit, each above its own floor and each total ending in 5 or 0. Two new sizes, 8 and 10 unit, fill the gap the anchors left, and 25 unit is added because the supplier quotes it. The finding this exposes. Wholesale on this desk is not a pricing problem, it is a buying problem. The price is set by what the trade will bear, so the only lever that makes it earn is the rate the salt is bought at: at RM56/unit a RM875 lot returns about RM73, at the RM48/unit already achieved on the 50 unit tier the same lot returns RM188. The market panel now says so in those words, and judges retail and wholesale against their own floors rather than one number that flattered neither.

Pricing becomes an engine, and the simulators are retired (26 Jul). The desk had two what-if boxes: one asked whether a supplier quote was good, the other whether a sale price was. Both answered a figure you typed in hopefully, one size at a time. They are gone, along with costBase(), and replaced by a Pricing tab that quotes every lot size the desk sells, driven by the book rather than by a table written once. The Workbench is now the Transaction tab, a label change only; the queue, the entry form and every internal name are untouched. Layer 1, cost. The rate is what the next unit costs, defaulted to the dearest tier on the live quote (RM56/unit, the 12.5 unit tier), because that is what restocking in the size usually bought actually costs; cheaper tiers are there to be chosen, never assumed. Onto it goes the shrinkage load: at 12.7% lost, every unit that reaches a customer must carry the ones that did not, so the effective cost is RM64.17/unit. Margin on the board is measured on that. The margin against the bare RM56 is shown as the headline figure and labelled the flattering one to distrust. Shrinkage is now priced in rather than absorbed. Layer 2, the taper. One flat margin cannot serve a desk where half-units clear above RM100/unit and 12.5 unit clears at RM66. Target margin runs 65% at 0.5 unit to 40% at 12.5 unit, logarithmic in quantity so the discount is steep over the first few units then flattens, over a hard 30% walk-away. There is deliberately no ceiling: the small end has been paid RM150 and RM210/unit without resistance, and a cap would have refused both. Layer 3, five signals, each worth a few points, summed and clamped to ±10% so no single week runs away with the price list. Today they read +9%: cover +4 (0.3 days), demand +3 (+217%), purchase cost 0, receivables +2, margin realised 0. Two are deliberate and must not be tidied. Demand counts units ordered, not shipped, because on a desk that keeps running dry an order you could not fill is still demand, while cover uses shipped units since that is what consumption means. The purchase-cost signal is asymmetric, a rise passed on in full and a fall at half weight, because plan P3 found the opposite habit here: discounts handed over faster than the savings meant to fund them. Shrinkage sits in the cost and is not also a signal, since counting it twice would lift every price for a loss already paid for once. A party overlay for loyalty, introductions and money outstanding is kept separate, capped at ±8%, and can never take a quote under the walk-away. Totals round to end in 5 or 0; the per-unit figure is derived and may carry sen. The finding is in the market panel. The desk has been paid RM84.90/unit across 119.81 unit, worth 24.4% on today’s effective cost, below the 30% walk-away. Small packs earn 36.6% at RM101.15/unit; bulk earns 16.1% at RM76.45/unit. For the realised bulk price to clear the floor unchanged you would have to buy at RM46.70/unit. Nothing on the tab books anything: a quote becomes a figure only when it is recorded on the Transaction tab. Stamped v138 rather than the v137 the instruction asked for, because v137 was taken earlier the same day by the cash, cover and policy work.

The desk starts looking forward (26 Jul). It recorded the past very well and said almost nothing about the next seven days. Every existing figure is unchanged: revenue RM10,172, margin RM3,655, receivables RM333 net, stock 2.82 unit, weighted average RM55.19. 1. Cash. P1 admitted the desk could not check whether its own 100 unit buy was affordable. It now reports the trading flow it can prove from rows already recorded: RM9,162 in, RM7,950 out, RM1,212 net, against RM520 still to come in and RM80 promised away. What it cannot know is what was in the bank before 26 Jun, so it reports a flow and says so rather than passing it off as a balance; set OPENING_CASH and every figure becomes a real position. 2. Cover. The shelf has 0.3 days left at the last fortnight’s 6 unit a day, and sits 13.43 unit below a new 15 unit reorder trigger. A stockout appears in no other figure here, which makes cover the one number that warns before the loss rather than after it. 3. The rules now bind. One setting for everyone is why the panel got ignored. Caps follow standing (1 unit retail, 2 unit associate) with a 10-day age rule that bites whatever the size; floors follow order size (45% singles, 40% mid, 37.5% bulk) because the cost and discount ladders run in opposite directions. Closed sales under floor are now one summary line rather than seventeen rows, since a banked price cannot be revisited, and the Workbench names a party already in breach before you record another sale to them. CS6-PER still reads as a breach, on three counts. 4. The two invisible leaks can now be recorded. Shrinkage was a plug: RM956, 26% of all margin ever earned, with nothing to say how much was chosen and how much was lost. Self-use or loss attributes it without touching the count. Turned away captures demand you could not serve, which until now left no trace at all. 5. Follow-up has a memory. Reconnect listed the same names every day whether or not you had called; each now shows when it was last contacted and what was promised, with a due list when a promise falls due. None of the four new entry types moves revenue, cost, stock or margin, all ride the existing queue, and all are idempotent under replay. Also: a tab now opens at the top instead of keeping the scroll position of the one you left.

Full audit: two real bugs, one missing colour, and the dead wood cleared (26 Jul). Every figure on the desk is unchanged and reconciles to the pre-audit baseline: revenue RM10,172, margin RM3,655 at 35.9%, receivables RM333 net, recoverable RM188, stock 2.82 unit, weighted average RM55.19. 1. The Ledger contradicted the receivables table. CJ4-BJ’s 28 Jun and 05 Jul orders were shown as Open · Advance when both are fully settled, and the receivables table rightly excluded them. The cause: those orders carry the balance in settledRM (RM50 and RM90) but their Linked amendment steps were written with cash:0, so the step-by-step replay never saw the money move and left the order open, while txStat read it as closed. Every other in-kind settlement on the desk puts the value on the step, as CJ4-OKR’s 09 Jul rebate does. The two steps now carry their RM50 and RM90, both cards close as Completed, and a systematic sweep of all twelve amended orders confirms no state disagreement anywhere else. Display only: the replay feeds no figure. 2. The Whiteboard had no accent colour. Nine of the ten tabs set their own --acc; plans was never given one and silently fell back to the Overview gold. It now has a chalk tone of its own, which suits a tab that sits outside the books. 3. Dead code removed after proving each item unreachable: the dlv and wbISO helpers and two orphaned locals; the .costcard rules, an orphan .warnnote b, and the four .todwrap/.todsel rules left behind when the time-of-day switcher went at v132; and six custom properties never read, --bg1 and --g1 to --g5. Checked and found sound: no duplicate element ids, no dangling handler, every roster code used and every used code on the roster, the provisioning ladder correct at 0/25/50/75/100, the stock walk footing to the count, and Chart.js already degrading gracefully when it cannot load.

The Network tree had a line that went nowhere (26 Jul). The horizontal bus joining the three partners was drawn as a free-standing rule at width:calc(100% - 150px) of the whole panel, which is a fraction of the container and has nothing whatever to do with where the boxes sit. On a wide screen it therefore ran hundreds of pixels past the outermost boxes at both ends, so the tree read as three nodes hanging off a bar that continued into empty space, and CJ4-OKR’s short 12px stem was lost against the overhang. The bus is now drawn by the child columns themselves: each column paints a 1px top border across its own width, the first column suppresses its left half and the last its right half, so the bar can only ever begin and end exactly on the outermost stems, at any width and for any number of partners. The flex gap is replaced by column padding so the segments meet without a break, and a lone partner draws no bus at all. New classes .nrow, .ncol and .nstem replace the inline styles. Presentation only: no figure, rank, rebate or attribution moves, and CJ4-OKR stays raised and first on the left.

Ten decisions on the Whiteboard, drawn from the ledger (26 Jul). The queue was empty, so no figure moves and nothing here touches the books. What is added is P3 to P12, a synthesis of the trading record into decisions that are still open. The through-line is that the desk has earned RM3,655 of gross margin and leaked most of it through three fixable channels: the bulk discount ladder is upside down (roughly RM30/unit given away to save RM8 to RM16/unit on the buy, RM1,123 forgone across five bulk orders, 31% of margin ever earned), shrinkage at 12.7% (RM956, 26%), and the SF6-KLC default (RM750, 21%). Alongside those: the small-pack floor is worth RM408 at RM120 on the same 19 unit already sold; CM6-HCM alone produced 19% of all gross margin from a single unrepeated order; CJ4-OKR bought RM80 and introduced RM2,090, a 26 to 1 ratio with nothing in writing behind it; 12 of 20 customers have bought once and three are now dormant past a fortnight; sourcing is 100% concentrated on SA5-BTR ahead of a RM4,000 to RM4,800 order; free-to-sell cover is 1.57 unit against 36 to 52 unit weekly trade; and RM1,240, 34% of margin ever earned, sits with counterparties. Every plan carries the figures it rests on, and all ten are filed as Idea, because they are decisions for you rather than decisions taken. P1 and P2 are untouched. Ageing rolled to 26 Jul: CS6-PER 12 days, CN6-WM 5, CD4-CS 1 and the SF6-KLC recoverable 18. No provisioning band moves and no figure changes, so receivables hold at RM333 net and the recoverable at RM188. The supplier recoverable reaches 100% provisioned on 29 Jul.

CJ4-OKR is Co-Founder, and the tree is redrawn to say what is actually true (25 Jul). The v132 tree hung the associates off him, which implied their trade runs through him. It does not: all three deal with you directly. The three now branch from one line off you, and standing is shown by position rather than by a false chain of command — he is placed first on the left and raised on a shorter stem, the associates set lower and to the right. A line beneath says so in words, so the drawing cannot be misread. His title changes from Principal to Co-Founder, held by him alone, in gold, with no rank number; the others stay Associate #1 and #2 by contribution. Nothing about rebates, attribution or the R1/R2/R3 streams moves.

An unknown-buyer bucket, one palette, and a Principal (25 Jul). 1. Unknown end buyers get a bucket, not a fold and not a name. Folding them into the reseller lost the distinction you actually want, so every onward sale to someone you never met now books to a single per-reseller bucket. The 17 Jul unit at RM115 and the 21 Jul 7 unit at RM580 sit there. You can now ask the question plainly: was that salt for him, or for someone else? CS6-BS-1-MK at Mont Kiara and CS6-BS-2-BK at Bandar Kinrara keep their own codes, because you delivered to them and know who they are. The Workbench defaults to the bucket and mints <reseller>-X automatically, so no stranger ever gets a code of his own again. His end-customer count reads 3, being two known and one bucket. No figure moves. 2. One palette. The four time-of-day bands and the rail switcher are gone; the desk is pinned to Register (classic), the palette of the original Salt Trading Register. The stored preference is cleared rather than left behind to puzzle a future reader. 3. CJ4-OKR is elevated to Principal. He was listed as an Associate at level R0, which put him on the same bench as the people he introduced. He now holds a tier of his own, held by him alone, sitting between you and the associates: the tree reads You, then Principal, then the associate bench branching off his level under the line “the bench he opened”. He carries no rank number, because a number invites comparison with a bench he does not sit on; the others are ranked #1 and #2 by contribution as before. His Diamond gem and the rebate ladder are untouched, and no rebate, figure or attribution changes — this is standing, not arithmetic.

Unknown end buyers stop being split, lots arrive by the unit, and the Register’s price charts come across (25 Jul). 1. The split rule is now explicit. A reseller’s onward sale is broken out to a coded end customer only where you delivered to that person yourself, which means CS6-BS-1-MK at Mont Kiara and CS6-BS-2-BK at Bandar Kinrara and nobody else. The two invented codes are retired: the 17 Jul unit at RM115 and the 21 Jul 7 unit at RM580 now fold into CS6-BS as single transactions, because a code for someone you never met adds a row to the network and tells you nothing. The Workbench field now defaults to “Not known — fold into the reseller” rather than demanding a name. No figure moves; the roster loses two entries. 2. A purchase now arrives by the unit. A lot used to be all-or-nothing: the moment the first unit landed, the whole lot entered stock and the cost basis, so 12.5 unit of cost could arrive with 5 unit of salt, and the balance could never be received afterwards. Lots now carry the units actually landed, and each part enters the basis at that lot’s own rate. The Order book counts only the balance still to arrive rather than the whole lot, and the ledger reads a part-delivered lot as Partial. Every historical lot is fully received, so no figure changes: 131.25 unit bought, RM7,200, average RM55.19. 3. An unpaid lot is a bill whether or not it has landed. In-transit lots were excluded from payables while the panel opposite called them “paid for, not yet received”. Payables now count them, and that panel is retitled “ordered, not yet received — paid or not”. 4. Dates are blank and must be typed. All three date fields opened pre-filled with the desk’s own date, which on a file opened days later is quietly wrong, and dates drive provisioning, the P&L month and the same-day rule. They are now blank and flagged, like the party. 5. Two things carried over from the Salt Trading Register. Its price-response charts now sit under the simulators: volume sold at each price, and revenue at each price. Its refusal to fit a demand curve is kept deliberately — there is nowhere near enough data, and a drawn curve invites decisions it cannot carry. Its rounding fault is fixed: it bucketed by rounded price then valued the bar at that rounded price, so RM108.33 showed short; revenue here sums the real totals. A reading beneath names your busiest price, your best-earning price, and what share of volume has gone below the floor. Its colour palette is added as a sixth theme, Register (classic), in the rail: near-black slate with the cool-blue and violet aurora and cyan-gold accents. Your time-of-day themes are untouched.

The Workbench coaches you while you key, and three tabs stop contradicting each other (25 Jul). Four changes, plus an audit register. 1. Pricing now runs off replacement cost. The entry form and the sell simulator judged every price against the book average, which flatters a sale that will ship from a dearer lot: RM55.19 where the shelf actually costs RM64. Both now lead with the replacement cost, what it costs to put the unit back, and show the book reading beside it. 2. A live pricing coach. As you type, the form reads the price against what it costs to replace the salt and against what that party has actually paid: it flags a sale below replacement cost and names the total that would clear the 20% floor, calls a best-ever or best-for-that-party rate, warns when you are discounting more than 10% below their usual, and warns when a price runs 25% above a regular’s usual rate, because steep rises are how loyal buyers are lost. A new party gets told the price is setting their anchor. It never blocks a record: a deliberate discount is a decision, not a mistake. 3. No dropdown starts on an answer. Party, order, kind, associate, end customer and “settles which order” all now open blank and must be chosen, and the party clears after every record so a second sale cannot inherit the first one’s buyer. The associate box also closes and clears, which quietly mattered: it stayed ticked, so a later R3 sale could be credited to an associate you never re-chose. A blank Total is now an error too; it used to silence the whole pricing pane and book a zero-revenue order that still drew real units. 4. Three tabs reconciled. The v126 pending fix had been applied to the headline figures only, so the Financials P&L read RM10,372 and the Customers tab the same, against the Overview’s RM10,172, and the Customers total row mixed a gross revenue with a net margin percentage. All three now net the pending tail: revenue RM10,172, cost of goods RM6,516.95, margin RM3,655, 36% everywhere. The amend pane also read two of CJ4-BJ’s orders as still owing RM140 and would have accepted a payment for cash settled in kind, because it replayed the amendment trail rather than the row; it now uses the same figures as the rest of the desk. And the Overview no longer calls RM1,010 “still to come in” when only RM490 is cash and RM520 was settled in kind.

A Whiteboard for plans (25 Jul). A tenth tab, and the first part of the desk that is deliberately not a record of what happened. Plans live here with a status of committed, idea, done or dropped and an optional date, and the tab leads with how many are live, how many have slipped and how many fall due inside a week. The discipline is the point: nothing on this tab touches revenue, cost, stock, receivables or margin, and nothing here is ever inferred into the ledger. A plan becomes a figure only when you record it in the Workbench as a real entry. You can add one in the browser and it rides the same queue file, tagged as a plan, which the overlay ignores outright, so it can never book itself or inflate the Workbench count; it shows as queued, not yet filed until I fold it in and synthesise it against the ledger on the next run. Seeded with your two: the 100 unit buy on Tue 28 Jul and the RM100 to RM150 repricing of 1 unit sales, each carrying the arithmetic and the caveat that goes with it.

Correction to the v125 note (25 Jul). That entry called the RM150/unit to CD4-CS the dearest sale the desk has ever booked, ahead of RM144/unit to CM6-HCM. Both halves were wrong. CH5-KLC paid RM210/unit for a half unit on 17 Jul, so RM150 is the best full unit rather than the best rate. And CM6-HCM was repriced to RM104/unit back at v19; the RM144 figure came from the superseded RM1,800 booking. The v125 wording is fixed. No figure anywhere else moves, and CD4-CS’s 57.3% margin is unaffected. Worth knowing before setting a ceiling: your proven top is RM210/unit on a half unit, not RM150.

CJ4-BJ squared off properly (25 Jul). You confirmed the two facts the desk had wrong: the 15 Jul cash was RM650, not RM600, and it all stood against the big order, because the 28 Jun RM50 and the 05 Jul RM90 were never settled in cash despite both deliveries going out. His order is therefore restored to its full 12.5 unit / RM850 with RM200 outstanding, reversing the v115/v116 resizing, which had rested on the phantom RM200. His true account: RM1,540 invoiced, RM1,200 cash in, 13.25 unit delivered. On your instruction the unpaid RM140 is offset against the big order rather than chased: you withhold 2.0588 unit (RM140 at his RM68/unit), that salt stays on your shelf, and the two old orders close. His deliverable drops from 12.5 unit to 10.44 unit. The position now reads: owed to him today 1.25 unit (paid for, not collected), pending 2.94 unit / RM200 (neither paid nor delivered, so it counts nowhere), and 4.19 unit to hand over when the RM200 lands, at which point every account between you is closed. Cash collected rises to RM9,162, revenue to RM10,172, margin RM3,655, 35.9%, and free to sell to 1.57 unit. Known conservatism: the withheld 2.06 unit still carries cost in the margin figure although it never leaves the shelf, understating profit by about RM113. Left as it stands rather than patched, because the same field on the CS6-PER package covers salt that genuinely did move, and a blanket engine change would corrupt that.

CJ4-BJ audit: a payment that never happened (25 Jul). You asked why he showed a deferral when he had paid you nothing more, and the audit found the cause. The RM200 booked as received on 23 Jul was never paid; it is the balance he still owes on his 15 Jul order. It is reversed, and the RM200 (2.94 unit at his RM68/unit) moves to pending. His account now reads: invoiced RM1,350, received RM1,150, taken 13.25 unit, with RM200 outstanding but unbilled because nothing has moved against it. What you owe him by weight falls from 3.46 unit to 0.51 unit, so with 2.82 unit counted, free to sell returns to +2.31 unit and the oversold breach clears. Cash collected falls to RM9,112. The correction also exposed an engine defect. An order was dropped from revenue and cost only when it was wholly pending; a part-pending order still carried its pending tail in both. CJ4-BJ is the first such order under this engine, and it was inflating the book by RM200 of revenue and RM161 of cost. Revenue and cost of goods are now taken net of the pending slice on every order, as the rule always intended. Revenue restates to RM9,982, cost of goods to RM6,363.61, and margin firms to RM3,618.39, 36.25%. No other order has a pending tail, so nothing else moves.

A record price, and the shelf goes short (25 Jul). Committed from the queue: a new customer, CD4-CS at Cheras Selatan, took 1 unit at RM150 with nothing paid and the unit handed over. At RM150/unit it is the dearest full unit the desk has sold, though not its best rate: CH5-KLC took a half unit at RM210/unit on 17 Jul. Against the RM64/unit lot it earns a 57.3% margin. Because it is delivered-unpaid it lands straight in receivables: trade AR rises to RM490 gross, RM332.50 net of the ladder, with CD4-CS at 0 days and so unprovisioned. Revenue moves to RM10,182, collections are unchanged at RM9,312, and the margin firms to 35.9%. Two cautions. He sits exactly on the 1 unit credit cap, not under it, so there is no headroom for a second unit before he pays. And the unit leaves stock at 2.82 unit against 3.46 unit still owed to CJ4-BJ, so free-to-sell is now negative at −0.64 unit: the desk has sold salt it does not hold. That is a genuine boundary breach and is left flagged, not suppressed. Restock before promising another unit to anyone.

CR3-DAM settled his RM80 (25 Jul). Ledger cards redesigned (24 Jul). Three changes to the entry cards. And a long amendment trail now collapses its middle steps behind a tap-to-expand summary, from three interim steps up, so a heavily-modified order no longer sprawls. Opening and closing rows, figures and margins are unchanged.

Delivery audit corrections (24 Jul). Your annotated checklist confirmed all 37 deliveries went out, but flagged two as mis-stated. Correcting the over-stated CJ4-BJ delivery widens the gap: the ledger now implies 21.15 unit on hand against 3.82 unit counted, so self-use and shrinkage rises to 17.33 unit. Two more flags, CN6-WM (possible default) and the CS6-PER package, await your confirmation.

Stock recount to 3.82 unit; a 14.11 unit audit gap flagged (24 Jul). The full walk: opening 4.90 unit plus 131.25 unit received (SA5-BTR 106.25 unit, SF6-KLC 25 unit) is 136.15 unit in; against 118.22 unit drawn (112.22 unit delivered plus the 6 unit loan) the ledger implies 17.93 unit on hand, so the count leaves a 14.11 unit gap booked as self-use and shrinkage, about 10.8% of all salt bought. SA5-BTR purchase timing reconciled to the payment record (24 Jul). Against your exact payment log (13 payments totalling RM5,600), two purchase dates were corrected: the RM700 / 12.5 unit lot moves from 09 Jul to 08 Jul (paid 08 Jul 21:28), and the 25 unit (RM1,400) moves to 22 Jul, where its payments of RM700, RM400 and RM300 all fell, having been split across 21 and 23 Jul before. CJ4-BJ loyalty rate reverted (24 Jul). At your call the RM200 tranche goes back to his standard RM68/unit, so it buys 2.94 unit, not the 4 unit of the loyalty rate. His 15 Jul order returns to 9.71 unit / RM660 at RM68/unit; delivered 9.47 unit, so 0.24 unit is owed to him by weight again, down from 1.29 unit.
