Three queued deals committed, shelf refilled (24 Jul). From the queue: a 6.25 unit buy from SA5-BTR at RM400 (RM64/unit), received and paid, refilling the empty shelf; and two cash sales, CS6-BS-1-MK 2 unit for RM220 (RM110/unit) and CE4-CHE 2.5 unit for RM230 (RM92/unit), both delivered and completed on the new lot at 41.8% and 30.4%. Net of the 4.5 unit sold, the shelf is counted at 1.75 unit; 1.29 unit of that is still owed to CJ4-BJ, leaving 0.46 unit free to sell, so the oversold position clears. Revenue rises to RM10,032 and cash collected to RM9,232. The RM64 lot is dearer than the RM56 tier, so the shelf cost rises to RM64/unit.

CJ4-BJ given a loyalty rate on the RM200 (24 Jul). As a most-loyal customer his closing tranche is repriced from RM68/unit to 4 unit for RM200 (RM50/unit). His 15 Jul order is now 10.76 unit for RM660 (6.76 unit at RM68 plus 4 unit at RM50), a blended RM61.34/unit; he has taken 9.47 unit, so 1.29 unit is owed to him by weight, deferred until restock. This lifts what you owe him from 0.24 unit to 1.29 unit, so with an empty shelf you are oversold by 1.29 unit. RM50/unit sits below the RM56 lot cost, so the tranche runs at a small loss, and his effective margin across all dealings eases from 32.1% to 27.8% (RM375 on RM1,350).

CJ4-BJ settled to weight, not price (24 Jul). Correcting the earlier reprice: squaring is measured in units owed or advanced, so his rate stays RM68/unit. He paid exactly RM200 (RM660 in all, being 9.71 unit at RM68) and took the 3.22 unit left on the shelf, for 9.47 unit delivered against 9.71 unit paid. His 15 Jul order is resized to 9.71 unit / RM660 at RM68 and the unpaid balance cancelled; 0.24 unit is still owed to him by weight, carried as a deferred delivery until restock. His effective margin across all dealings is 32.1% (RM434 on RM1,350). The shelf is now empty, so with 0.24 unit owed you are oversold by 0.24 unit, and self-use and shrinkage has climbed to 16.18 unit (about RM886), which warrants a physical check.

CJ4-BJ squared off his open order (23 Jul). He paid a further RM200 and took 3.46 unit, the 0.51 unit he was owed plus 2.94 unit for the new money. His 15 Jul order is repriced to the 9.71 unit / RM660 he has actually taken and paid, now Completed, and the undelivered 2.79 unit / RM190 at RM68/unit is carried to a fresh pending order rather than cancelled. Across all his dealings his effective margin is 32.1% (RM434 on RM1,350). A fresh count puts the shelf at 3.22 unit, all free to sell; the ledger implies 15.94 unit, so self-use and shrinkage now reads 12.72 unit. Revenue eases to RM9,582 and cash collected rises to RM8,782.

Network tab: a diagram of how it counts (23 Jul). The Network tab now carries a small themed diagram between the totals and the associate cards, spelling out the three streams and why each matters: R1 Bought (his own orders, no rebate), R2 Sold for you (onward sales booked to him, one free unit per RM500), and R3 Brought you (first-order value of each customer he introduces, one free unit per RM1,500). It shows the roll-up on one line, Made you = R1 + R2, with R3 kept to the side feeding the rebate and rank, plus a note on why folding R3 into the total would double-count the referred buyer. Explanatory only; no figure or logic moves.

Six completions and a recount (23 Jul). The deferred and pending book largely clears. CS6-BS took his 7 unit once the restock landed, and three pending orders completed together: CZ6-WM 1 unit at RM100, CA4-DAM 0.5 unit at RM50, and new Petaling Jaya buyer CR4-PJ 12.5 unit at RM830 (RM66.40/unit, a 15.7% margin that sits under the 20% floor). On the buy side the in-transit 6.25 unit landed and a fresh 12.5 unit at RM56/unit (RM700) came in paid, taking stock bought to 125 unit and the weighted-average cost to RM54.76. A physical count put the shelf at 5.5 unit, below the 8.0 unit the ledger implied, so self-use and shrinkage rises to 13.9 unit and is worth a look. Revenue rises to RM9,772, cash collected to RM8,582, and margin to about RM3,467, 35.5%; free to sell is 4.99 unit and pending falls to a single 5.74 unit tail on CJ4-BJ.

CS6-PER is back under the cap (22 Jul). At your call the exemption is dropped: his repriced package no longer sits outside the 1 unit credit cap, so the 3.7 unit he holds delivered and unpaid reads as a breach again, consistently in the Boundaries register, the Order book and the Advances panel. This reverses a change I made in v108 on a misread of which line you were flagging. No figure moves, because the exemption only ever governed the cap warning, not the RM290, which was aged and provisioned throughout. Boundaries now read two breaches — his margin floor and his cap — alongside two watches.

Four bookings, the pending rule, and clearer sections (22 Jul). Half the lot landed and the shelf is healthy again. SA5-BTR delivered 6.25 unit of the 12.5 unit lot at RM56, the other 6.25 unit due within hours and still in transit; stock is counted at 10.25 unit and, against 7.51 unit owed out, free-to-sell turns positive at 2.74 unit, so the oversold breach clears. CR3-DAM took his standing unit on credit at RM80, payment promised Friday, so it moves from pending to an advance and revenue rises to RM8,792; he is at the 1 unit cap. Two new pending orders, both agreed with nothing moved: CA4-DAM 0.5 unit at RM50 and a new Petaling Jaya customer CR4-PJ 12.5 unit at RM850. Rolling the desk to 22 July ages two positions — CS6-PER to 50% provisioned and the SF6-KLC recoverable to 75% — so net receivables read RM275 trade plus RM187.50 recoverable. And two things you asked for: pending orders now carry no date and sit at the very bottom of the ledger; and each section leads with a bolder, accented heading so the blocks read distinctly instead of blurring together.

Design audit: text stays inside its box (22 Jul). You caught long cells breaking out of the Boundaries panel; the cause was a blanket rule that forced every table cell onto a single line, so any long note ran past the rounded border. Text columns now wrap while the number columns stay on one tabular line, so nothing spills out anywhere on the desk. In the same pass: KPI subtitles wrap instead of truncating with an ellipsis, so no figure is hidden; a card sitting inside a frosted section no longer frosts twice; and long codes or words break cleanly rather than punching out. All nine tabs were re-rendered and checked — no overflow, no missing or malformed value, and the figures are unchanged.

The boxes line up now (22 Jul). The glass coat made an older inconsistency plain: panels carried five different corner radii and several different paddings and top-margins, so stacked boxes like Boundaries and Deferred deliveries did not share an edge. Every panel now sits on a single 14px radius, a common padding and a uniform 14px gap between boxes, with the slim callouts at 12px. Purely fit and finish; no figure or logic moves.

A liquid-glass coat, a clock-driven palette, and a boundary fix (22 Jul). The desk is restyled in frosted glass: every panel, the rail and the tables now sit on translucent, blurred layers with a soft gloss edge, while the figures stay crisp. The colour shifts with the time of day across four dark bands — dawn, day, dusk and night — chosen automatically by the hour, with a Theme switch in the rail to pin one or leave it on auto (your choice is remembered). And a fix you spotted: the Boundaries register was flagging CS6-PER for the 1 unit credit cap on an order that is explicitly exempt from it, unlike the Order book and Advances panel which already excused it. The scan now honours the exemption, so breaches read 2 rather than three — the margin floor and the oversold shelf.

Overview becomes a full digest, the rebate rule bites, and the desk reads in Segoe (22 Jul). Three things you flagged. First, the Overview now carries the headline from every tab: a digest strip for free-to-sell, pending and deferred units, cash collected, buyer concentration and salt in transit, then a Reseller milestones card and the latest ledger lines, sitting above the accounts that were already there. Second, the rebate rule you set: an earned free unit now offsets an outstanding advance before it is ever handed out as salt. CS6-BS had earned a second unit and was carrying a RM90 advance, so the two net off: his RM90 clears in kind and he owes nothing, with no salt leaving an already-oversold shelf. Only where the associate holds no advance does the button queue a free-salt redemption, and it no longer reads “unit unit”. Trade receivables ease to RM340 gross, RM267.50 net across CS6-PER and CN6-WM; revenue, cash and margin are untouched, since the sale was earned when the salt first moved. Third, the desk named a font it never loaded, so served over the launcher it fell back unpredictably; it now uses a native Segoe UI stack that renders the same, offline, every time.

The R2 party trap is closed, and two Network mislabels are corrected (22 Jul). Three fixes in the associate corner, no figure touched. First, the reseller trap: on an R2 sale the top Party field was still shown and then silently thrown away, because the sale books to the associate, not to that field. It now hides in R2 with a note pointing you to End customer, and in R3, where the buyer really is the party, it stays and is relabelled Buyer (referred). Second, the tree node badge counted, for an ordinary associate, only the end customers he had resold to, ignoring anyone he had referred, so CS6-PER read "0" despite having introduced CH6-TBC; it now counts resells and referrals together, and he reads 1. Third, the second line on each node showed R1, R2 and so on, which looked like a revenue stream but was really a rank by contribution, colliding with the genuine R1/R2/R3 labels in the cards below; ranks now read #1, #2, while the founder stays R0, a role rather than a rank. So, to answer the two questions this settles: R1/R2/R3 classify a line, not a person. Every associate keeps the same three streams: bought (R1), resold (R2), referred (R3). CS6-PER trades on R1 and R3, CS6-BS on R1 and R2. And CS6-PER does have a customer, CH6-TBC, which the badge was simply failing to count.

Three entries: a restock, a pending customer, and a forward reseller sale (22 Jul). All came through the queue overnight. SA5-BTR was paid RM700 for 12.5 unit at RM56 up front but has not delivered, so the lot sits in transit, out of stock and out of the weighted average until it lands. CZ6-WM opens at Setiawangsa with 1 unit at RM100 agreed and nothing moved, so it is pending and touches no figure. CS6-BS resold 7 unit for RM580 (RM82.86/unit), paid in full with delivery deferred until that restock arrives; it books to him as an R2 line with the end customer left in the general bucket, since the reseller did not name his buyer. That resale carries him past two rebate rungs at once, to 2 free unit earned and RM400 from a third. Revenue rises to RM8,712 and cash collected to RM7,602, while stock on the shelf holds at 5 unit because nothing physically moved. The forward sale did trip a boundary, exactly as it should: the desk now owes out 7.51 unit against 5 unit on hand, so Free to sell reads minus 2.51 unit and stands in the register until the restock covers it. Two caveats carried in the open: the reseller sale was entered with a name in the top party field that the R2 booking discards, which is a trap worth closing, and the end customer stays a code until he is named.

The referred sale lands, and the refer stream opens (21 Jul). The buyer held back yesterday for want of a name arrived through the queue: CH6-TBC, 2 unit at RM115/unit, paid and collected together, so it folds into the opening as a single line at the RM56 lot cost. It is the first sale booked to a refer (R3) line rather than a resell, and the machinery added an hour earlier did exactly what it should: the sale books to the buyer, while the introduction credits CS6-PER, whose three streams now read RM1,240 bought, nil resold and RM230 referred, leaving him RM1,270 short of a free unit. Revenue reaches RM8,132 and stock falls to 5 unit, of which 4.49 unit is free to sell. One caveat carried in the open: the location was entered as TBC, so that code suffix is a placeholder rather than a place. It stays as minted, because a code is canonical once issued and re-keying a party is a deliberate act, never a silent tidy-up.

Associates can be appointed, and two new customers open (21 Jul). You could not add an associate because the desk decided who was one by looking for people who had already made an R2 sale, so a pure referrer never appeared and the dropdown offered no way to add anyone, unlike the end-customer field beside it. That was backwards. The role is now one role, appointed first and traded under after, because R2 and R3 classify a revenue line rather than a person: the same associate resells on one line and refers on another, each earning its own rebate, 1 free unit per '+'RM500 resold and per RM1,500 referred. One definition of an associate now feeds both the Network tab and the Workbench: appointed, or has resold, or has referred, or is the founding referrer. CS6-PER is appointed, and a Stream switch on the entry pane sets whether a sale books to the associate with an end customer behind him, or to the buyer with the introduction credited to him. Trade: CI4-OKR opens at Old Klang Road with 2 unit at RM92.50/unit, paid and delivered together; CN6-WM opens at Sepang with a 0.5 unit advance at RM100/unit, wholly unpaid and inside the credit cap. Revenue reaches RM7,902, stock falls to 7 unit and receivables rise to RM430 gross. Two entries from that conversation are deliberately not booked, for want of a name and a quantity.

The boundaries are now enforced, and they hold (21 Jul). The rules the desk trades by were scattered: the credit cap was checked on a new order but not an amendment, the margin floor only in a simulator, and the commit boundary existed only as a sentence in a briefing. They now live in one evaluator read by both the entry pane and a standing Boundaries register under the headline figures on Overview, so a rule reads the same as you type it and as you review it. Five are enforced: the 1 unit credit cap, counted across everything a customer holds rather than one order at a time; the 20% margin floor on every priced sale; free to sell, which cannot go below what is already owed out; and the provisioning ladder on both trade receivables and the supplier recoverable. Alongside them sit the commit risks: a provisional entry the desk can see will probably read differently once judgement is applied, whether that is cash that may belong to an older order, a same-day amendment that will fold into the opening, or a sale still costed at the weighted average rather than its traceable lot. Nothing is blocked except arithmetic impossibility, because a ledger records what happened rather than preventing it; a breach is warned once and then stands in the register until it is actually resolved. Switching it on found three live items straight away: CS6-PER holds 3.7 unit delivered and unpaid, nearly four times the cap, which is the same RM290 seen as salt rather than money; that customer's 08 Jul package still reads 0% margin; and the SF6-KLC recoverable is half provisioned at 13 days.

Recorded entries fold into the desk at once, and can be undone (21 Jul). Until now an entry sat in the queue looking inert until I committed it, so the desk you were reading was always one step behind the business you were running. Every entry now lands in every figure immediately: revenue, cash, receivables, payables, stock, cost and margin all move as you press Record, and the entry appears in the Ledger with a Provisional tag. A banner rides above all nine tabs reading how many entries are recorded but not yet committed and how much cash they carry, so an unbanked figure is never mistaken for a banked one. Undo sits on the banner and against each row in the Workbench. It works by dropping the entry and replaying what is left on top of the committed source, so it can never leave the desk half-changed, and replaying is idempotent no matter how many times it runs. The mechanism is an overlay, not a rewrite: the committed ledger is held pristine and the queue is layered on it at load, which is why a refresh keeps your entries and why the existing watermark still retires each one the moment I bake it in. What a commit is still for is judgement the browser does not have: late cash belonging to an older order, a same-day settlement folding into the opening, the right cost basis for a sale. A provisional figure is the naive reading; the committed one is the true one, and any difference between the two is now explained in this log rather than appearing silently.

The last supplier balance is cleared: RM200 to SA5-BTR (21 Jul). The 20 Jul lot came in at RM56/unit with RM500 handed over on collection and RM200 left owing. That balance is now paid, so the lot reads Paid and Received, and the supplier bills table empties: nothing is owed to any supplier for the first time since the book opened. This is also the first entry to arrive through the route added an hour earlier, a Payment recorded against a supplier lot rather than passed to me in a message, which is the amend pane working on the buy side as intended. No other figure moves, because a lot enters the cost basis when it is received, not when it is paid: stock holds at 9.5 unit, the weighted average at RM54.47/unit, and revenue and margin are untouched. Cash out rises by RM200.

Supplier lots can now be amended (21 Jul). The amend pane listed customer orders only, because its order list was filtered to sells before it was drawn, so a lot already in the book could not be paid down, topped up or written off from the desk. A Side switch now sits above the list: Customer order behaves exactly as before, Supplier lot lists the purchase rows under the same E-codes the Ledger tab uses, so a code means one thing across the desk. The Kind list follows the side, because a lot cannot be fulfilled, rewarded or linked; it is paid down, received, or defaulted on. Progress comes off the row itself, since purchases carry no amendment trail, and the pills relabel to Received and Not received so a lot no longer reads as though it were being delivered to someone. Payments are capped at the cash outstanding and receipts at the units still to come, each ignores the other field with a warning rather than silently booking it, and marking a default warns that the money already paid becomes a recoverable rather than stock. The live case is the RM200 still owed on the 20 Jul SA5-BTR lot, which now has a route through the queue instead of a message to me. No figure moves: this is the entry surface, not the ledger.

One pending order delivered, one cancelled (21 Jul). CA4-DAM paid and collected his half unit, so it moves out of the pending book and into revenue at the RM56 lot cost. CC5-OKR cancelled his unit before any cash or salt moved. Cancellation was a state the Workbench could record but the ledger could not hold, so it is now a proper terminal state: a cancelled order counts nowhere, drops out of the pending book, and reads Cancelled on its card rather than lingering as though still live. The order remains visible with its cancellation step, because a deal that was struck and called off is worth remembering. Pending falls to 6.74 unit / RM470, stock to 9.5 unit.

Restocked, and a first sale off the new lot (21 Jul). 12.5 unit in from SA5-BTR at RM56/unit, received in full with RM500 paid on collection and RM200 still owed, which now shows as a supplier bill in the Order book. Purchases can carry a part payment for the first time; a lot that is in but not fully paid reads Open · Advance rather than pretending to be settled. Then 2.5 unit at RM250 out to CE4-CHE, paid and delivered together, drawn from that lot at its true RM56 cost. Entered as a new party, but the code its name and area generate was already his, so it books as his second order rather than creating a duplicate. The shelf goes from nil to 10 unit, stock cost moves to RM56/unit as the remnant is all new lot, and the weighted average edges up to RM54.47. The desk date rolls to 21 July.

Queued order committed: CA4-DAM, 0.5 unit at RM50 (20 Jul). Half a unit at his RM100 anchor, agreed with nothing paid and nothing handed over, so it joins the pending book and touches no figure. It is his second order, and the first arrived through the self-clearing queue: the previous entry had already dropped itself, and this one carried its own stamp. Pending orders now stand at 8.24 unit worth RM610 across four customers, against nil stock.

The queue clears itself (20 Jul). Committing entries left you to press Clear queued afterwards, and forgetting meant the same order could be booked twice. Each entry now carries the moment it was recorded, and this file carries a commit watermark; anything queued at or before it is dropped the next time the desk loads, with a line saying how many were cleared. Entries recorded after a commit survive untouched, so nothing is lost if you keep working while the ledger is being updated. The button stays for clearing something you would rather not send.

CS6-BS part-paid his advance: RM17 of RM107 (20 Jul). Paid the same day the unit was handed over, so it folds into the opening rather than trailing a movement behind it. He still owes RM90, which is the whole of his exposure and keeps him at the 1 unit credit cap. Receivables fall to RM380 gross and RM307.50 net; cash collected rises to RM6,307. Revenue and margin are untouched, since the sale was already earned when the salt moved.

Queued order committed: CC5-OKR, 1 unit at RM90 (20 Jul). Agreed at his usual rate, with nothing paid and nothing handed over, so it sits as a pending order and touches neither revenue, cost, receivables nor stock. It arrived through the Workbench and reached this ledger without a copy-and-paste, which is the hand-off working as intended. Pending orders now stand at 7.74 unit worth RM560 against nil stock on the shelf.

Captions that were telling you nothing (20 Jul). Version control carried a signpost explaining that Names & IDs had moved and how to use it — stale in three details and unnecessary the moment the button sits on every tab. Gone, along with a line on Network restating what the cards below it already show. The Financials note about “amounts folded into later orders” described a mechanism retired an hour earlier, so uncollected now reads simply as delivered salt awaiting payment.

CJ4-BJ’s three orders now tie out (20 Jul). His RM140 of old balances had been cleared by treating 1.5 unit of the 15 July order as already delivered — but that salt was invoiced once on the June and July orders and again inside the RM850, so RM140 of revenue and RM81 of cost were counted twice and his account showed RM250 outstanding against a true RM390. The money is now recorded as what it was: of the RM600 handed over on 15 July, RM140 settled the two older balances, which close as ordinary late payments, and RM460 stands against the new order. His account reconciles to the ringgit — RM1,540 invoiced, RM1,150 received, RM390 to come. Revenue, cash collected and margin are all unchanged, because nothing was ever really earned twice; only the split moves, with deferred salt down to 0.51 unit and his pending order up to RM390. Pending values are also now taken from the unrounded units, so they no longer drift by a few sen.

Full audit, two new capabilities, and a new coat of paint (20 Jul). An independent review of the whole desk surfaced 22 findings; the material ones are fixed. Queue files and the clipboard now carry codes only, even while names are shown. Clearing the queue writes an empty file so cleared entries cannot be re-committed. If the desk server dies mid-session, Record says so and falls back to a download instead of pretending. The vault will not overwrite a newer copy without asking, and codes from the vault file can never rename ledger parties. A half-typed entry survives locking or showing names. Zero-value orders, the ageing clock and badge margins are all tightened. NEW: a Financials tab — monthly and financial-year P&L with provisions, and cash against invoiced — and the Ledger gains search and filters by party, state and month. DESIGN: every section now carries its own accent colour through the active tab, headings and rules — deliberate, not monotonous, never loud — the rail shows live counts of open positions and queued entries, and the Pending pill is finally readable. The one flagged item left alone: the folded-advance RM140 sits in revenue on both its original orders and the order that absorbed it — that is the audited 17 Jul model, changed only on request.

The vault is translated back onto the current codes (20 Jul). Unlocking decrypted perfectly and still showed nothing, because the vault was written under the retired C##-Xn ids and never re-keyed when the codes changed in July, so every key missed. A translation table now maps the old keys onto the current codes as the vault opens, for display only, and all 18 names land. Saving re-encrypts under the current codes, after which the table is redundant. Nothing had been lost at any point: the ciphertext was intact throughout and only the labels on it were stale.

Your browser’s vault is the one that counts (20 Jul). Moving the vault into a file introduced a fault: on load the desk read the browser copy and then overwrote it with the file’s, so an older file could quietly replace names added since. The browser copy now wins, the file being there for portability and for a browser that has never seen the vault; where they differ the desk says so and Save reconciles them. Unlock also reports what it actually found — how many names filled, and any keys that do not match a code on the ledger — so an empty panel can be told apart from a lost vault. Keys are codes, never names, so the report reveals nothing.

Names & IDs: unlocking no longer moves the codes (20 Jul). Unlocking silently re-derived every code from the vault names and overwrote the map the desk displays, so simply reading a name could rename every party on screen while the ledger underneath kept the original id. Unlock now only decrypts. Codes are minted on Save, and only for a party that has none: an existing id is canonical and is never overwritten, because the data keys on it. If a name implies a different code, the desk says so and leaves the code alone rather than acting on it. The panel is down to what it needs: Unlock becomes Lock, Save re-encrypts and locks behind itself, and Show names exists only while unlocked. Export appears only when the desk is opened without its server, which is the one case where nothing else can save the vault.

The Inventory chart no longer depends on being online (20 Jul). Chart.js was loaded from the internet alone, so with no connection the whole Inventory tab fell over rather than merely losing its chart. It now falls back to a local copy in assets\, and if that is missing too it leaves a one-line note where the chart would be while the rest of the tab renders as normal. The copy came from the old salt_command_files folder, which is gone: Windows treats such a folder as joined to the page that created it, so deleting it in Explorer would have taken the desk with it.

Names and IDs save themselves too (20 Jul). The vault had the same flaw as the queue: changes lived in the browser, and the encrypted blob only survived because it was pasted back into this file by hand. It now travels the same road as the queue, to salt_vault.json beside the desk, so Save and Generate persist by themselves and the codes survive a cleared cache or a different browser. Only the encrypted envelope is written; the passphrase never leaves the browser and is stored nowhere. The blob is also out of this file entirely, so the desk now carries no name data at all and can be shared or screenshotted without a second thought.

The queue saves itself, with nothing to click (20 Jul). Granting folder access was the wrong shape of answer: a browser re-asks for it roughly every session, which is a recurring tax for something that should be invisible. Since the desk is served locally anyway, it now simply hands the queue to its own server, which writes salt_queue.json into this folder directly. No permission prompt, no Connect button, no downloads to tidy: one file, overwritten each time, including when the queue is cleared. Opened by double-clicking instead, it still falls back to a download and says so. The whole file-permission apparatus is gone, and the folder is down to three files: the desk, the launcher and the server.

The desk can be served, which fixes the hand-off properly (20 Jul). A page opened by double-clicking has no real origin, so the browser bars it from writing to its own folder. Opening the same file over a local address removes that restriction. start_desk.bat now starts a small local server, using Python or Node, whichever is installed, and opens the desk on it; serve_desk.js is the dependency-free server behind it, bound to this machine only. Served that way, the Workbench shows Connect folder and writes salt_queue.json straight beside the desk. Double-clicked, it quietly falls back to the download route and says so. Same file either way, and nothing else changes.

Record saves a file you can actually see (20 Jul). The folder-write route added an hour earlier turned out to be barred: a browser refuses folder access to any page opened straight from a folder, which is how this desk is opened. Record now downloads salt_queue.json instead, which a local page is allowed to do, and the daily run reads it from the download\ folder beside this desk, where the browser is set to save. Each file carries the whole queue, so the newest supersedes the rest and older copies can be binned. Save queue file repeats it on demand and Copy queue still puts the lines on the clipboard. The folder route stays in the code for the day this is served over localhost, where it does work.

Record now actually hands the entry over (20 Jul). Clicking Record used to write to browser storage and nothing else: it looked saved, survived a reload, and yet the folder never changed, so the queue was invisible to the daily run while the header promised it would be “committed on the 9pm run”. A button cannot keep that promise on its own. Now Connect folder asks once for permission to this folder, remembers it between sessions, and every queue change writes salt_queue.json beside this file for the run to read. Where the browser refuses, the entry goes to the clipboard instead and the header says plainly that it is held in this browser only. No more silent queues.

Two entries committed, and pending orders stop counting (20 Jul). Queued from the Workbench: CR3-DAM takes 1 unit at RM80, agreed but neither paid nor handed over, and a stock count of nil. Committing the first exposed a dormant fault — revenue and cost of goods summed every row, so an order where nothing had moved still added RM80 of revenue and RM54 of cost. They now run off orders that have actually moved, matching the rule the receivables column already followed. No past figure changes, because until today no order had ever sat in a pending state. The nil count is authoritative, so the 1.9 unit that was on the shelf books as self-use, taking it to 11.4 unit.

The stock walk adds up again (20 Jul). The reconciliation on the Inventory tab counted the 6 unit loan twice — once inside “Sold and delivered”, which already carried it, and again on its own line. The walk therefore closed at −4.1 unit while the footer said 1.9 unit. The sold line now shows deliveries only, so opening → received → sold → loan → self-use lands exactly on the counted 1.9 unit. No figure anywhere else moves: the loan was always handled correctly in the totals, only the displayed walk was wrong.

Pending orders record properly; same-day deals stay one line (20 Jul). A blank or zero total used to read as Paid, which hid genuine pending orders — agreed, nothing moved. Fixed, and the preview now says so in words. An order that is paid and delivered together confirms it will record as a single line, and an amendment dated the same day as its order folds into the opening rather than becoming a separate movement.

Pricing and Input become one Workbench (20 Jul). Recording a transaction is now a guided form that covers every kind of ledger entry — a new order, an amendment to an existing one, or a stock count — with dropdowns, quick-set buttons and validation, and a live preview of the Payment, Delivery and State it will produce before you commit it. The pricing side keeps only the buy and sell simulators; the quote card and price matrix are retired. The desk header now also carries the version and the time it was last updated, not just the date.

Network reads in plain English (20 Jul). The three streams are named for what the associate actually did — Bought from you, Sold for you, Brought you — with the R1/R2/R3 codes demoted to a quiet tag. Each now carries a real count (onward sales, customers introduced) instead of restating its own label.

Margin moves under the total (20 Jul). Each total now carries its margin as subtext beneath it, in ringgit and per cent, turning red under 20%. That made the separate deal-margin table a duplicate, so it is gone. The tab intro is cut to a single line.

Advance delivery to CS6-BS (20 Jul). Handed over 1 unit at RM107, unpaid — an advance delivery, so he owes the money. Revenue rises to RM7,367; stock eases to 1.90 unit, of which only 0.83 unit is free to sell against the 1.07 unit still owed out. Receivables now RM397 gross (RM324.50 net — this one is too fresh to provision). He is at the 1 unit credit cap. Also: a simple order that is part-done now names its state precisely, Open · Advance or Open · Deferred, matching the amended orders.

Clean copy (18 Jul). Retired the old free-text change log now that every amendment is structured: the superseded events lists are gone from all seven orders, along with the unused status-detail builder and a stale style rule. Old entry references (E5, E12, E25, E16) that pointed nowhere are rewritten as plain dates, so the only entry codes in the desk are the live, clickable ones. Nothing on screen changes and no figure moves — the source is simply tidier.

Ledger lines align, and movements show what changed (18 Jul). Quantity, price, total and margin now sit in four aligned columns across every line, so cards read consistently. Each line shows what actually moved at that step in full strength, with the carried-over figure greyed — so a delivery on credit shows the units bright and the money grey, and the later payment flips it. Set-offs are now named for what they are: Rewarded for an associate’s free unit, Linked orders where one order settles another. Every entry carries a code, and a linked reference is clickable straight through to that entry.

Opening and closing now read as distinct roles (18 Jul). A single-line order is a closing — the deal is done, shown with a green “Closed” marker. An order that moved through steps reads Opened (ice) → movements → Closed (green), and an order can go straight from Opened to Closed with nothing in between. An order still live shows Open in ice, no closing yet. The role marker and a coloured left-edge make each line’s part in the order obvious at a glance.

Simple orders show a single line (18 Jul). An order that opened and closed in one moment, with no movements in between, now shows just its one line (tagged Completed) instead of a separate opening and closing. Only orders that actually moved through steps show the full open → movements → close bracket.

Ledger reads as open → movements → close (18 Jul). Each order is now a single card. The opening entry shows it as first booked; any movements that followed sit in an indented, recessed panel beneath, on a connecting rail; and a closing entry appears once the order completes. Orders still open stop at their latest movement, with no closing line. Simple orders are just their opening line. The type scale is cut to two sizes and the columns tightened, so parent and amendment no longer look alike.

Ledger: separate Payment, Delivery and State, and structured amendments (18 Jul). The status is now three columns — Payment, Delivery and State (Pending, Completed, or Open split into Advance and Deferred). Each amendment under an order is a fully-structured row showing the cash and salt that moved that step, with its own pills derived by replaying the order; the note is kept only when it adds something. The opening entry and earlier steps grey out, leaving the latest row as the current state.

Ledger amendments are now typed entries (18 Jul). Each change under an order reads as its own dated row beneath the parent, in the same columns, and carries a type: Fulfilment (a payment or delivery that progresses the deal), Modification (a change to quantity, price or amount), Cancellation (a void, ending in a refund or completion) or Set-off (netted against another order, with a “see…” reference). Amendments run oldest to newest, each with its date, and the Payment / Delivery / Order pills are filled only where the note actually states them.

Ledger updates read as a trail, not filler rows (18 Jul). When an order has changed over time, its original row now dims as a superseded starting point, and the changes hang beneath it as an indented update thread — a connector line rather than look-alike entries. The latest update is highlighted as the current state, tagged “now”, with earlier steps muted. So a part-paid, part-delivered order reads at a glance as: where it started, and where it stands.

Inventory rebuilt around the shelf (18 Jul). The tab now opens on hero cards — stock on hand, free to sell (red if oversold), stock value at the latest lot cost, average cost, and self-use / shrinkage as its own headline — then two collapsible sections: Stock reconciliation (opening to on-hand, with the self-use gap explained) and Lots and sourcing (each purchase and whether it is in the cost basis), with the movement chart kept. The per-deal margin table has moved to the Ledger, where it sits with the rest of the per-transaction detail; Inventory is now purely about stock.

Navigation regrouped (18 Jul). The sidebar now clusters by purpose: Position (Overview, Order book, Inventory), Relationships (Customers, Network, Ledger) and Actions (Pricing, Input). The transaction tab is renamed Input, and the changelog is renamed Version control, kept subtle at the foot of the rail.

R0’s free unit booked as his rebate (18 Jul). CJ4-OKR’s 1 unit was previously a one-off Diamond gift; under the new rule it is simply his earned R3 rebate (his referrals crossed RM1,500), so it is now set off against that free unit, exactly the way CS6-BS’s unit clears against his resell rebate — every associate is treated the same. The RM80 was already in revenue, so revenue is unchanged at RM7,260; the only change is that the unit shifts from a waived gift to a rebate set-off, so in-kind expense eases from RM170 to RM90. His rebate now shows as fully applied. The Diamond badge is the sole distinction, awarded at your discretion, and carries no change to how the rebate works.

Every associate, the same ledger; rebate by value (18 Jul). Each associate now keeps the same three-stream ledger — Buy (R1), Resell (R2), Refer (R3) — because any of them can do all three; R0 and R1 differ only in the numbers. The free-unit rebate is now by value, per stream: 1 unit per RM500 of resell and 1 unit per RM1,500 of referral (own buys earn nothing). So R0 earns his unit through R3 crossing RM1,500 (referrals RM1,840), and R1 through R2 crossing RM500 (resold RM520) — the old 1-unit-per-5-unit rule is retired.

Network: one name, R0 first, sharper badges (18 Jul). Everyone in the network is now an Associate — the referrer and the resellers share the term, distinguished by level (R0, R1, R2…), and R0 leads the list. A split order now counts correctly toward referral credit: orders on consecutive days are treated as one introduction, so CG5-SB’s 26+27 June units count together (R3 RM400, up from RM100). The Diamond rank is now a bold gem pill that stands out, and star ratings are ready as coloured pills as associates earn them.

Network: every partner on equal footing (18 Jul). Reseller 0 (the referrer) now stands alongside the resellers — in the tree diagram (marked Referrer) and as a full card, not a footnote. A third metric, Referral (R3), joins Direct (R1) and Indirect (R2): a referrer’s R3 is the first order of each customer they introduced. The tab now reads diagram → an overall summary (partners, total R1/R2/R3) → one collapsible card per partner: collapsed shows code, role, what they made you, customer count and rebate status; expanded gives the R1/R2/R3 breakdown, rebate and full ledger. Ready to grow as you add partners.

Order book: hero cards and collapsible sections (18 Jul). Each half now opens with three hero cards carrying the headline numbers, coloured by direction: green for what is owed to you (cash net, salt in transit, refund due), warm for what you owe. Every section below is collapsible: those with items open with a count in the header, empty ones stay tidily collapsed and marked “none”, so the tab opens on what actually needs attention.

Order book restructured by counterparty (18 Jul). The tab now has two clear halves — Customers then Suppliers — each with the same four positions: cash owed, salt owed, refunds, and pending orders. Only open (part-done) and pending (agreed, nothing moved) items appear; completed orders are settled and drop off. Each half opens with a one-line summary. The near-empty debtor-ageing bar chart is removed — the ageing now lives as columns (age, provision, net) in the cash-owed table. Emphasis is disciplined: bold for headings, codes and totals; amber only for attention (an advance over the 1 unit cap), red only for risk (salt owed beyond stock on hand).

Old IDs fully retired (18 Jul). With your name vault re-exported under the current codes, the last bridge is gone: the desk now holds only the current codes, with no old-to-new mapping table anywhere. Your re-keyed encrypted vault is baked in and unlocks directly. Nothing else changes.

One ID convention throughout (18 Jul). The desk now carries the current codes (CS6-BS, CJ4-BJ, CS6-PER and so on) as the only identifiers — in the live data and in this changelog history; every earlier internal key has been purged. Your encrypted name vault still works unchanged: on unlock, old keys are mapped to the new codes automatically, so names resolve as before. No figures move — this is a pure relabel. (To retire the last mapping table, unlock and Export the vault once so it re-keys to the new codes.)

Order book: the full five-part view, new ageing ladder (18 Jul). The Receivables tab is now the Order book, laid out in order: Accounts receivable (advance deliveries — salt out, cash not in), Debtor ageing with the provisioning table and chart, Accounts payable (supplier bills for salt delivered to you, plus any refund you owe a customer), Deferred delivery (paid, salt still to hand over, to the amount paid), and Pending orders (taken but neither paid nor delivered). Each section leads with a plain definition. The provisioning ladder is revised to 0-3 days 0%, 4-7 25%, 8-13 50%, 14-20 75%, 21+ 100% (applied across the whole desk), so a very fresh debt is no longer written down. A netted prior advance now counts as goods already delivered, valued at the originating order’s rate: CJ4-BJ’s RM140 becomes 1.5 unit, so his effective delivery is 7.75 unit, leaving deferred 1.07 unit and pending 3.68 unit.

Receivables becomes a full owed-both-ways view (18 Jul). The tab now splits into Owed to you and Owed by you. Owed to you keeps the aged, provisioned Advance sales (salt delivered, not yet paid) plus the supplier refund, with the ageing chart. Owed by you gathers Deferred sales (paid, not yet delivered) shown in unit and their RM value at the order price, alongside supplier bills (cash payables) — currently none outstanding. The definitions are rewritten in plain terms: Advance means a customer owes you money, Deferred means you owe a customer salt.

Overview reworked to a decision view (18 Jul). The Stock on hand KPI now shows only what you truly owe out — deferred deliveries (paid ahead), not unpaid orders. The old average buy cost is replaced by Stock cost: the cost of the salt actually on the shelf, at the latest lot’s RM48/unit (the remnant is all from the 50 unit bulk lot). Receivables stays net of provisioning, with the gross-versus-net split spelled out. The old “bought X, margin Y” footer is promoted into a Margin headline KPI, and the glance row is a symmetrical six cards. The full customer table is replaced by a “Who to look after” shortlist: those to go out of your way for (loyal or high-margin) and those who need a nudge (no order in 21+ days).

New KLCC customer logged; desk cleaned up (18 Jul). Booked a new direct customer CH5-KLC at KLCC: 0.5 unit at RM105 (RM210/unit), paid and delivered same day. Revenue rises to RM7,260; stock eases to 2.90 unit. Separately, a full dead-code sweep: removed a duplicate, unreachable copy of the Names & IDs panel (the source of the extra vault buttons), an old Overview renderer, the retired free-text entry box and its parser, three unused data blocks and some redundant styles. No change to any figure, tab or button you actually use.

Reseller 1 onward sale (17 Jul). Your reseller CS6-BS sold 1 unit at RM115 to a new end customer, delivered at his own place so the code inherits his location. Paid upfront and delivered same day per the true-reseller terms — Completed. Revenue rises to RM7,155; stock eases to 3.40 unit.

Full ledger audit and rebuild (17 Jul). Every transaction re-booked on a three-axis model: a Payment leg (Paid / Partial / Unpaid) and a Delivery leg (Delivered / Partial / Undelivered), with the order state derived as Completed / Pending / Open — Open being Advance (delivered, unpaid) or Deferred (paid, undelivered), split exactly at the order’s RM/unit and shown with timeline sub-rows. Receivables are now Advance legs only and are aged and provisioned (written off 25/50/75/100% by age); pending unpaid-and-undelivered orders sit off the books. Key corrections: CJ4-BJ booked at actuals RM600 plus an RM850 order that absorbs his RM140 advance (Deferred 0.51 unit); CM6-HCM repriced to RM1,300; the CS6-PER package booked as a 12.5 unit sale and squared against his 12 May loan, his live order repriced to 6.25 unit / RM490; the SF6-KLC RM750 default 50% provisioned. New reseller layer: Reseller 0 (referral) versus true reseller, a manually-awarded Diamond rank, and a network-revenue read. Revenue RM7,040, net receivables about RM683.

Margin on a delivered, real-cost basis; sub-20% flag; cleaner badges (16 Jul). Margin is now booked on the whole order at the actual lot cost where known, not the blended average. So CS6-PER, sold at RM60/unit from the RM48 bulk lot, reads its true 20% instead of a flattered 55% (the old figure charged only the half-delivered cost, at the RM54.26 average, against the full revenue). Any customer or sale under a 20% margin is now flagged thin. Removed a duplicate 1 unit cash sale under CC5-OKR, whose real purchases are 2 unit, so revenue eases to RM7,000. Badges restyled to a subtler dot-and-label.

Reseller tiers, rebate and customer badges (16 Jul). Indirect revenue is now a single R2 (the reseller manages the sale on your stock); the old A/B split is gone, and a downstream who starts dealing with you directly simply becomes an R1 customer. Each reseller earns 1 unit free per 5 unit sold under R2 (redeem or set off), shown on their ledger. Resellers carry a star rating by share of your total sales (1★ ≥10%, 2 ≥30%, 3 ≥50%); CS6-BS is about 6%, so unrated. Customers now carry badges on the Customers tab and the order-habits table: Loyal, Regular, New, Dormant, and a High-margin flag for the top quarter by margin. The selected reseller card is re-coloured for legibility.

Reseller de-duplicated (16 Jul). A node booked separately turned out to be the same person as your reseller CS6-BS, so the two are merged into one, now with two downstream customers (CS6-BS-1-MK and CS6-BS-2-BK). No figures change. Tidy the vault so this person has a single entry.

Deferred vs advanced deliveries split (16 Jul). The Overview no longer files every part-done order under “deferred”. A line is deferred only when payment has run ahead of delivery, so you owe goods (CJ4-BJ: paid ahead, 4.75 unit to hand over). It is advanced when delivery has run ahead of payment, so they owe you money (CS6-PER: 6.25 unit taken on RM200 of RM750, RM550 outstanding). A separate deliverability gap line flags that 11 unit of orders sit against 4.40 unit on hand. The stale CS6-PER settlement card is removed.

Martin delivered; two more sales (16 Jul). CM6-HCM’s 12.5 unit was handed over, so it now draws stock and books its cost: stock falls to 4.40 unit and the headline margin steps down as the deferred cost is realised (his traceable lot cost is RM48/unit, so his real margin is wider than the wavg shows). Sold another 1 unit to CC5-OKR for RM90, paid. And a further R2 sale of 1 unit for RM120 through your reseller CS6-BS to a second end customer (CS6-BS-2-BK). Revenue RM7,090, collected RM5,960; stock is very low at 4.40 unit against 11 unit still owed out, so a restock is now urgent.

Add tab: guided entry and stock count (16 Jul). A new Add tab replaces free-text with a form: pick Sell or Buy, choose the party from a dropdown (or + Add new with name and location), then quantity, total and payment. A separate Report stock count box logs a fresh weight. Entries queue in your browser and are committed on the daily sync; the desk cannot save to file by itself.

ID carries the location; the name does not (16 Jul). The on-desk ID now includes the location code (for example CF3-LK) everywhere; the revealed name is just the person’s name, without the location. Margins are aligned to the delivered-quantity basis, so per-customer and per-lot margins now sum to the headline total (a paid-but-undelivered order shows its cost deferred until handover). The desk date is rolled to 16 Jul; SLT-CM6-HCM’s 12.5 unit delivery is due today.

Overview entry box removed, a sale booked, generator hardened (15 Jul). The free-text Add a transaction box is gone from the Overview, which now opens on your position. Recorded a 1 unit cash sale at RM90 to CC5-OKR (revenue RM6,880, stock 18.90 unit). The ID generator now falls back to the plain ID for anyone not yet named in the vault, so it never shows a stub code; combined with the earlier fix for keys saved under the old ID format, re-open Changelog, Unlock and Generate to apply clean codes.

ID generator (15 Jul). Set your vault names as Name (Location), then press Generate IDs in Changelog and the desk mints short codes from them: C for your own customers, R{n}A for someone a reseller sells to on your behalf, R{n}B for a referral, each as first letter plus name length and a location code (multi-word places use initials, so Lanai Kiara becomes LK; otherwise the first three letters). The location shows only here in Changelog, never on the rest of the desk; names stay encrypted, and the eye still reveals full names for delivery.

Network tab (15 Jul). A new tab maps your selling network: you at the top, resellers below as clickable nodes. Click one to open its reseller ledger - what they have made you (direct R1 vs indirect R2), their downstream customers, and every onward sale you were paid for through them - plus a reseller ranking. First reseller is CS6-BS with one downstream customer.

Position at a glance, expanded (15 Jul). The Overview now carries two new reads: Reseller performance (what each reseller has made you, split into direct R1 and indirect R2, and how many customers they run) and Customer order habits (each buyer’s order count, total and average size, and how long since their last order), so reliance and buying rhythm are visible at a glance.

Statuses tidied across the desk (15 Jul). Every status now reads as one of paid, partial, unpaid, default or in-kind (barter and set-offs are in-kind, the supplier refund is default, the credit tag is dropped), in the ledger, receivables and the entry queue alike. Non-sale movements are also hidden from the ledger, so CS6-PER shows only its latest real sale; the old debt and package rows stay in the data for stock.

Orders pending payment cleared (15 Jul). Both open orders are resolved, so that panel is now empty. CS6-BS’s 1 unit order resolved into their single credit unit already on the books (the RM120 log-1 unit); it is not a second purchase, so no figures change. CE4-CHE let their 2 unit / RM185 order lapse past the 48-hour window, so it is dropped. Revenue holds at RM6,790, receivables RM950, stock 19.90 unit.

Reseller revenue split, and a top unlock (15 Jul). Sales now carry a revenue category: R1 (direct, a customer buying for their own use), R2A (indirect, a reseller manages the sale while you supply and deliver the stock, and they collect and pay you) and R2B (indirect, a referral who pays you directly). First entry: CS6-BS managed a 3 unit sale (RM285) to end customer CS6-BS-1-MK, booked R2A; the stock and delivery are yours, the reseller holds none. Only what you receive is recorded (RM285); their onward margin is not tracked. Revenue rises to RM7,440, collections to RM5,660, stock eases to 19.90 unit (now oversold by about 3.6 unit against what is owed out, so a restock is needed). Also added: a Reveal names control at the top of the desk. Enter your passphrase to turn every ID into its real name across all tabs for delivery, then Lock to hide them again; it decrypts in your browser only. The Network tab that reads these categories is the next step.

Two customer records merged (15 Jul). A second record turned out to be the same customer as CS6-BS ("Fiq"): the 12 Jul RM95 cash sale and the 15 Jul RM120 credit unit now both sit under CS6-BS, and the duplicate is retired from the roster. Figures are unchanged (a relabel only); the Customers tab now shows one record for this buyer instead of two. He remains distinct from CS6-PER.

New customer booked, and CJ4-BJ balances netted (15 Jul). The held 1 unit / RM120 credit sale is booked to a new customer, CS6-BS (distinct from CS6-PER), at the 1 unit credit cap. For CJ4-BJ, his RM140 old credit (RM50 residual + RM90 weekend unit) is set off in-kind against 1.5 unit of the salt owed to him: his receivable falls to RM200 (the order balance) and what you owe him falls to 4.75 unit. Trade receivables now RM950 (CJ4-BJ 200, CS6-PER 550, CJ4-OKR 80, CS6-BS 120), total due RM1,700 with the RM750 refund, stock 22.90 unit, and you remain slightly oversold (about 0.6 unit short of what is owed out).

Supplier refund now counted as a receivable (15 Jul). The RM750 due back from SF6-KLC (paid for a lot that never arrived) is no longer just a side-note: it shows as a refund-due line in Receivables and is included in total amounts due to you, now RM1,720 (RM970 trade + RM750 refund). It stays flagged as recoverable pending the settlement meeting, and the ageing chart remains trade-only.

CR3-DAM paid (15 Jul). His RM80 credit unit is settled the same day it was delivered, so it leaves receivables: collections rise to RM5,375 and receivables ease to RM970 (CJ4-BJ RM340, CS6-PER RM550, CJ4-OKR RM80). His 1 unit credit cap is clear again.

CJ4-BJ 12.5 unit order (15 Jul). Sold 12.5 unit for RM850 (RM68/unit): RM650 paid, RM200 outstanding, and 6.25 unit delivered with 6.25 unit still owed. Revenue rises to RM7,085, collections to RM5,295, receivables to RM1,050 (CJ4-BJ now RM340). Stock eases to 23.90 unit; with 25 unit now owed out (CM6-HCM 12.5, CS6-PER 6.25, CJ4-BJ 6.25), free-to-sell turns negative (about −1.1 unit): you are oversold and must restock to deliver in full.

One desk, consolidated (15 Jul). This is now your single dashboard. A new Customers tab shows the top-buyer share, the top three combined, a Herfindahl concentration index and the margin earned per customer. The buy and sell simulators now take a total in RM plus a quantity in unit instead of a price per unit, so you enter a deal the way you quote it (for example RM700 for 12.5 unit) and the desk derives the per-unit. The parallel Salt Desk VI file is being retired so there is one desk to maintain.

CR3-DAM took 1 unit on credit (15 Jul). A 1 unit pack was delivered on credit at RM80/unit, dated 15 Jul. Revenue rises to RM6,235 and receivables to RM850 (CJ4-BJ RM140, CJ4-OKR RM80, CS6-PER RM550, CR3-DAM RM80); collections are unchanged at RM4,645. Stock eases to 30.15 unit (11.40 unit free, 18.75 unit still reserved for the deferred deliveries). RM80 is your Preferred-tier anchor and floor selling price, about a 32% gross margin at the RM54.26 cost; CR3-DAM is now at the 1 unit credit cap, the fourth open debtor and a third line at or below the RM100 anchor.

Buy and sell simulators (14 Jul). Two what-if tools on the Pricing tab. The buy simulator takes a quote (price/unit and quantity) and shows the blended average cost it would give, plus how much you would need to buy at that price to reach a target cost. The sell simulator takes a proposed price and shows the margin, markup and profit, with a traffic-light against your tiers: closest few 20% (25% markup), regulars 35% (54% markup), everyone else 50% (100% markup). Both read your live average cost (RM54.26/unit); nothing is saved.

Opening stock priced and folded into cost (14 Jul). The pre-record opening stock (4.90 unit) was carrying an unknown cost; it is now valued at your opening rate of RM64/unit and included in the weighted-average, which rises from RM53.71 to RM54.26/unit. Note this is a cost-basis change only: self-use, owed-out and shrinkage never touch the average — those are outflows, and the average is fixed by what you paid on the way in. The slightly higher cost lifts the price floors a touch; the RM1,350 loyal-25 unit guard still does not bind.

Physical count, and a free-to-sell figure (14 Jul). A stocktake put stock on hand at 31.15 unit (from the ledger’s 31.25 unit; the 0.1 unit gap books as a little more self-use). The Stock figure now shows the split: 12.4 unit free to sell against 18.75 unit reserved for the two deferred deliveries (CM6-HCM 12.5 unit, CS6-PER 6.25 unit). No change to revenue, collections or receivables.

Entry moved onto the Overview (14 Jul). The transaction box now sits at the top of the Overview, so the desk opens ready to record a deal without changing tabs; the standalone Add-transaction tab has been retired to keep the navigation lean. Type an entry and the figures below update at once.

CS6-PER delivery brought to halfway (14 Jul). A further 1.75 unit went to CS6-PER, taking his delivered total to 6.25 unit of the 12.5 unit; 6.25 unit is still owed. No cash moved — he still owes RM550, with a further payment expected soon (amount to be confirmed). Stock eases to 31.25 unit; revenue, collections and receivables are unchanged.

Corrected a customer ID (14 Jul). A customer’s ID was corrected so its mnemonic letter matches the real name held in your vault; this buyer is now CJ4-OKR. A relabel only: the 1 unit / RM80 credit sale and the RM80 in receivables are unchanged, just carried under the corrected ID across the ledger, roster and key table.

The 50 unit landed, and three deals moved (14 Jul). The 50 unit lot arrived and the RM800 balance was paid: it now sits in stock and in the average cost, which falls from RM61.33 to RM53.71 across 87.5 unit received. CM4-SK (new) bought 12.5 unit for RM825, paid and delivered. CS6-PER’s 12.5 unit / RM750 order was activated: RM200 paid (RM550 outstanding) and 4.5 unit delivered, with 8 unit still owed. Revenue rises to RM6,155, collections to RM4,645, receivables to RM770. Stock stands at 33 unit (ledger-implied — a physical count would confirm it), of which 20.5 unit is spoken for: CM6-HCM’s 12.5 unit (still awaiting delivery) and CS6-PER’s 8 unit. The lower cost also eases the price floors. Two orders (3 unit) remain pending payment.

Fixed a role label in the key table (14 Jul). Two customers were wrongly shown as Supplier in the private key table, because the check matched the letter “S” anywhere in the ID rather than only at the start. It now matches only the supplier prefix, so they read correctly as Customer. Labels only; no figure, ledger entry or price is affected. Your suppliers remain just the two: SF6-KLC and SA5-BTR.

Removed an unrecognised spot sale (14 Jul). The 11 Jul anonymous 0.5 unit / RM60 one-off (an unrecognised spot buyer) was struck from the ledger at your instruction — you did not recognise it. Revenue eases to RM4,580 and collections to RM3,620; receivables are unchanged at RM220. Because the count on hand is still zero, that half-unit now reads as self-use/shrinkage rather than a sale, nudging the inferred figure to 8.40 unit.

First payment in, first goods in transit (14 Jul). CM6-HCM paid in full for his 12.5 unit (RM1,800, at RM144/unit), delivery Thursday 16 Jul: the order leaves the pending panel and becomes a paid-but-undelivered sale — revenue and cash are recognised (revenue rises to RM4,640, collections to RM3,680), but the 12.5 unit is held back from stock and self-use because it has not been handed over, so you now owe him 12.5 unit. Separately, a 50 unit lot at RM48/unit is on part-payment and in transit: RM1,600 of RM2,400 paid, the RM800 balance recorded as a memo only (your instruction), and the lot excluded from stock and the RM61.33 average until it arrives. That lot is earmarked to deliver CM6-HCM. Receivables unchanged at RM220; three orders (15.5 unit) still pending payment. Margin is temporarily flattered: CM6-HCM’s cost is deferred until delivery.

Orders pending payment, and an empty shelf (14 Jul). Stock is restated to zero, so the desk now leads with a restock call carrying the full supplier ladder. Four orders taken but not yet paid or delivered (CS6-BS 1 unit/RM100, CS6-PER 12.5 unit/RM750, CE4-CHE 2 unit/RM185, CM6-HCM 12.5 unit/RM1,300, totalling 28 unit / RM2,335) sit in a new orders-pending panel, deliberately kept out of stock, revenue, receivables and margin until they are fulfilled on payment. The supplier quote is refreshed: 25 unit at RM1,300 (RM52/unit) is now the sharpest step, while the 50 unit break moved dearer to RM2,400 (RM48/unit). No live figure changes: revenue RM2,840, receivables RM220, wavg cost RM61.33.

Navigation and copy, cleaned up (12 Jul). The seven flat tabs became a grouped sidebar (Money, Stock, Sell, with the Changelog set apart), so the daily screens read as a set rather than a wall of pills; on a phone it folds back to a compact row. The wordier panels were cut to the essentials: the same figures, far fewer words.

Pricing tab, rebuilt around a quote (12 Jul). The tab now opens on a single quote card: pick a customer and type the units, and it returns the total (rounded to end in 5/0), the price per unit and the margin at once. Picking a known customer auto-selects their usual tier from the median price they have actually paid; new or walk-in buyers default to Standard, and you can override the tier in one click. Cost is no longer five boxes to maintain: every tier now prices off a single cost/unit that follows your ledger weighted-average automatically (with one optional override). The full matrix, price curves and shareable cards still exist, tucked into a collapsible Details section. No pricing maths changed: totals still end in 5/0, per-unit still falls with size, and the loss guard still floors every price at cost + your minimum margin.

Supplier update (12 Jul). SF6-KLC, who holds your RM750, was found to have had an accident; an in-person meeting has been requested to settle the outcome. Nothing has moved yet, so the RM750 stays a recoverable write-off and no figure changes. Best case is a full RM750 refund, which would fund another 12.5 unit from SA5-BTR at RM700 (a plan, not yet a purchase). The default panel wording was softened to reflect the accident rather than a walk-away.

PDPA hardening (12 Jul). Real names no longer appear anywhere in this file. Every transaction now carries its SLT ID directly; the old plaintext key table is replaced by an encrypted vault. In the Changelog you can set a passphrase and the names you enter are encrypted in your browser (PBKDF2 + AES-GCM); the passphrase never leaves your machine, and only the resulting blob is stored. Unlock it any time to read the key for that session. The signpost that a key existed was also removed from the footer. No figures changed: revenue RM2,840, receivables RM220, stock 1.56 unit.

Two cash sales & two new customers (12 Jul). CA4-DAM (new) took 1 unit at RM100, paid.
